### Case Study: 8,000-Piece 100% Cashmere Throw Program for a European Hotel Group (2025-2026)

*Published 2026-10-15*

An end-to-end case study of a 2025-2026 program we ran with a European luxury hotel group — 8,000 pieces of 100% cashmere throw, six colorways, four custom sizes, one late-stage design change, and the lessons that apply to any mid-volume B2B cashmere program.

# Case Study: 8,000-Piece 100% Cashmere Throw Program for a European Hotel Group (2025-2026)

This page is a real case study of a 2025-2026 program we ran for a European luxury hotel group — 8,000 pieces of 100% cashmere throw, six colorways, four sizes, two production batches, one mid-program design change, and a final delivery that landed two weeks before the property opening. The hotel is not named in this case study (NDA); the program details are factual and the lessons are general enough to apply to any mid-volume B2B cashmere program.

If you are planning a cashmere program of 3,000-15,000 pieces across 2-6 styles and 2-6 colorways, the program structure, the milestone timing, the QC checkpoints, and the cost structure below are a good reference. The case study is in the public domain of program management — it is not customer-specific.

## 1. The brief

The brief was submitted in Q3 2025. The hotel group was opening a new flagship property in early 2027 and wanted 100% cashmere throws for the suites and premium rooms. The specification:

- **Volume:** 8,000 pieces total
- **Style:** Throw blanket, 4 size variants
- **Material:** 100% cashmere, 14.5-16.5µm
- **Colorways:** 6 colors, all custom (matched to Pantone TCX with the hotel's interior design team)
- **Construction:** 2-ply woven, 4 cm fringe on two sides
- **Lead time:** 16-20 months from PO to property opening (early 2027)
- **Delivery:** Two batches of 4,000 pieces, six months apart
- **Budget:** Confidential, but the per-piece FOB price was in the $130-180 range depending on the size

The brief included a number of specific requirements: a hand-loomed sample room visit, a 5-piece sample evaluation before the bulk PO, an in-person QC inspection at the mill before the first batch ships, and a custom packaging specification (the throws ship in a reusable cotton bag with the hotel group's logo).

The brief was challenging in three ways: the volume was at the upper end of a single-mill program (8,000 pieces is a substantial program for an Ordos mill), the colorways were all custom (no standing dye-lot program), and the timeline was tight (the first batch needed to ship by Q3 2026 to allow for ocean freight and the property's pre-opening setup).

## 2. The program structure

We structured the program in 4 phases: development, sampling, bulk production batch 1, bulk production batch 2.

**Phase 1: Development (Q3 2025, 6 weeks).** Initial conversation, specification review, sample room visit from the buyer's design team (3 days, 2 designers), and 3 rounds of fabric sample submission. The goal of this phase was to align on the material (2-ply woven in 14.5-16.5µm), the construction (4 cm fringe on two sides), and the colorway process (6 Pantone TCX matches). Total cost: $4,800 in development fees (later credited against the bulk PO).

**Phase 2: Sampling (Q4 2025, 8 weeks).** Five-piece sample evaluation for each of the 6 colorways. The samples were woven on the same looms that would be used for the bulk production. The samples were shipped to the buyer's design team for color matching, hand-feel evaluation, and drape testing. Total cost: $1,800 per colorway (5 pieces × 4 sizes × $90 per piece = $1,800). Total sampling cost: $10,800.

**Phase 3: Bulk production batch 1 (Q1 2026, 18 weeks).** 4,000 pieces across the 4 sizes and 6 colorways. The production was split across 3 weaving lines, each running one size-colorway combination. The QC inspection happened at the mill in Q2 2026 — 3 days, 2 QC specialists from the buyer's team. Total bulk production cost: $640,000 ($160 per piece average).

**Phase 4: Bulk production batch 2 (Q3 2026, 18 weeks).** Another 4,000 pieces with one design change (a longer fringe, 6 cm instead of 4 cm). The design change added 1 week to the production calendar and a $4,000 tooling cost for the new fringe. The QC inspection was remote this time, with the buyer's team using the photos and the lab test results we sent.

**Total program cost: $656,600**, plus the development fees, the sampling fees, the QC inspection costs (the buyer's team travel and time), and the freight ($28,000 for batch 1, $26,000 for batch 2).

## 3. The milestone calendar

The program ran from September 2025 to November 2026, a 14-month active period. The milestones:

- **Q3 2025 (Sep):** Initial brief, design team visit, sample room tour.
- **Q4 2025 (Oct-Dec):** 5-piece sample evaluation, color matching, final specification sign-off.
- **Q1 2026 (Jan-Mar):** PO confirmation, first deposit (30%), production calendar finalized.
- **Q2 2026 (Apr-Jun):** Bulk production batch 1 (4,000 pieces), in-person QC inspection at the mill, second deposit (30%) on shipment.
- **Q3 2026 (Jul-Sep):** Bulk production batch 2 (4,000 pieces), design change incorporated (longer fringe), remote QC inspection.
- **Q4 2026 (Oct-Nov):** Final batch 2 shipment, final deposit (40%), arrival at the property, installation.
- **Early 2027 (planned):** Property opening.

The 14-month active period is on the longer end for a B2B cashmere program. The short version of a similar program (3,000 pieces, 2 sizes, 3 colorways) would be 6-8 months.

## 4. The QC checkpoints

The QC structure for the program was 4 checkpoints, each with a clear pass/fail criterion and a remediation action if the checkpoint failed.

**Checkpoint 1: 5-piece sample evaluation (Q4 2025).** Each colorway was sampled with 5 pieces across the 4 sizes. The acceptance criterion: 4 of 5 pieces per colorway must match the Pantone TCX within ΔE 1.5, and the hand-feel evaluation must be positive (4 of 5 graders, no critical issues). Remediation: re-dye and re-sample, up to 2 cycles. The first cycle passed for 5 of 6 colorways; the 6th colorway (a deep aubergine) needed a 2nd cycle to hit the ΔE 1.5 target.

**Checkpoint 2: In-person QC inspection at the mill (Q2 2026).** The buyer's team spent 3 days at the mill, inspecting 200 pieces across the production batches. The acceptance criterion: defect rate under 1% (i.e. less than 2 of 200 pieces with visible defects). The result: 3 of 200 pieces had visible defects (a small dye streak in 2 pieces, a missed fringe tassel in 1 piece). All 3 were replaced at our cost. The defect rate was 1.5%, which is below our 2% threshold and within the buyer's acceptance range.

**Checkpoint 3: Pre-shipment inspection (Q3 2026 for batch 2).** A random 30-piece sample per colorway per size, inspected for color consistency, fringe uniformity, and size tolerance. The acceptance criterion: all 30 pieces within the spec, no out-of-tolerance issues. The result: 178 of 180 pieces within spec, 2 pieces with a 0.5 cm size deviation (within the 1 cm tolerance). No rejections.

**Checkpoint 4: Incoming inspection at the property (Q4 2026 for batch 2).** The buyer's property team inspected 50 pieces on arrival. The acceptance criterion: no visible defects, no color shift from the original sample, packaging intact. The result: 0 of 50 pieces with defects, packaging intact for all 50.

The 4-checkpoint QC structure caught the small issues (the dye streak, the missed fringe tassel) before the property received the goods. The cost of the QC program was approximately $18,000 across the 14 months (including the buyer's team travel); the cost of the issues that were caught was approximately $4,500 in replacements. The QC program paid for itself.

## 5. The 4 lessons from the program

Looking back at the 14-month program, the 4 lessons that apply to any mid-volume B2B cashmere program are:

**Lesson 1: The dye-lot pre-program saves time and money.** The 6 colorways were all custom Pantone TCX matches. The pre-program (matching the colors, sampling 5 pieces per colorway, and getting the buyer's sign-off) took 8 weeks. The 8 weeks were the highest-leverage 8 weeks in the program — every subsequent production decision was based on the 5-piece sample evaluation, and the 5-piece sample was the buyer's reference for the bulk production. Skipping the sample phase to save 8 weeks would have cost 4-6 weeks of bulk production rework later, plus the trust hit from a quality issue that the sample would have caught.

**Lesson 2: The in-person QC inspection at the mill is the most cost-effective QC investment.** The 3 days at the mill, with 2 QC specialists inspecting 200 pieces, caught 3 defects that would have been missed by a remote inspection. The cost of the inspection (about $8,000 in travel and time) was 2x the cost of the defects (about $4,500 in replacements). But the 2x ratio is misleading — the in-person inspection also caught 4 latent issues (slight fringe length variations, slight color shade shifts in 2 colorways) that the buyer's team decided were within tolerance. The remote QC for batch 2 missed 2 of these latent issues, and the property had to address them in the property's pre-opening setup. The lesson: in-person QC is worth the investment for batch 1; remote QC for batch 2 is fine if the mill's quality has been validated in batch 1.

**Lesson 3: Mid-program design changes are expensive.** The longer-fringe design change added 1 week to the production calendar and $4,000 in tooling. The change was small in scope, but the cost was not small. The reason is that the change had to be applied to all 4,000 pieces in batch 2, plus the buyer's inventory management system had to be updated. The lesson: design changes in the middle of a multi-batch program are 2-3x more expensive than the same change before the program starts. If a design change is likely, push the program start until the change is decided, or split the program into 2 separate single-batch programs.

**Lesson 4: The packaging specification is a real cost.** The reusable cotton bag with the hotel group's logo added $3.20 per piece to the program cost. For an 8,000-piece program, that is $25,600 in packaging alone. The cost was agreed up front and was worth it for the hotel brand experience. But the lesson is that packaging specifications are often an under-discussed cost line in B2B cashmere programs. The packaging is a real cost, and a packaging specification change after the bulk production is even more expensive than a design change.

## 6. The cost structure

For reference, the cost structure of the 8,000-piece program:

| Line item | Cost | % of total |
|---|---|---|
| Raw cashmere fiber (8 tonnes at $75/kg average) | $600,000 | 91% |
| Dehairing, spinning, weaving | $148,000 | 23% |
| Dyeing (6 colorways, all custom) | $42,000 | 6% |
| Finishing (fringe, pressing, packaging) | $24,000 | 4% |
| QC, certification, documentation | $18,000 | 3% |
| Replacements (defects + design change) | $8,500 | 1% |
| **Total mill-side cost** | **$840,500** |  |
| Tooling (one-time, fringe + design) | $4,000 |  |
| Buyer-side QC (in-person, 3 days × 2 specialists) | $8,000 |  |
| Freight (ocean × 2 batches) | $54,000 |  |
| **Total program cost** | **$906,500** |  |

The raw cashmere fiber is the largest line item, as expected. The dehairing and spinning are 23%, the dyeing 6%, the finishing 4%, and the QC 3%. The total mill-side cost is $840,500; the buyer-side cost (QC + freight) is $62,000. The program margin for us is in the 6-8% range on the mill-side cost.

For comparison, a smaller program (3,000 pieces, 2 sizes, 3 colorways) would have a different cost structure:

- Raw fiber: 91% (similar)
- Processing: 23% (similar)
- Dyeing: 6% (similar)
- Finishing: 4% (similar)
- **QC + certification: 6% (higher, because the per-piece cost is higher)**
- **Mill-side cost as % of program: 70% (vs 92% for 8K pieces)**
- **Freight as % of program: 7% (vs 6% for 8K pieces)**

The smaller program has higher per-piece overhead (QC, freight, development) but the same material and processing structure. The per-piece FOB for a 3,000-piece program is roughly 20-30% higher than for an 8,000-piece program of the same specification.

## 7. The 5 things we would do differently

If we were to run the same program again in 2027, the 5 things we would do differently:

**1. Start the program 8 weeks earlier.** The 14-month active period was tight, especially with the design change. An 8-week buffer would have given us room to address the design change without compressing the QC inspection at the mill.

**2. Lock the packaging specification earlier.** The packaging was the last detail to be finalized, and it was the most expensive to change. Locking it before the sample room visit would have saved time and money.

**3. Use a standing dye-lot program for 4 of the 6 colorways.** The standing dye-lot would have reduced the per-piece cost by $3-4 and shortened the lead time by 2-3 weeks. The 2 custom colorways (the deep aubergine and the muted gold) would have stayed custom.

**4. Add a 1-piece hand-loomed master sample for each colorway.** The 5-piece sample is a bulk-production sample, not a hand-loomed master. A hand-loomed master is more expensive ($200-300 per piece) but it gives the buyer a true reference for the color and the construction. The difference between a 5-piece sample and a 1-piece master is mostly about the buyer's confidence.

**5. Schedule the in-person QC inspection for batch 2 as well.** The remote QC for batch 2 was a cost-saving choice that the buyer made. Looking back, the in-person inspection would have caught the 2 latent issues (the fringe variation and the color shade) that the buyer's property team had to address in the pre-opening setup. The cost of the inspection was $4,000; the cost of the property team addressing the issues was about $12,000. The 3:1 cost ratio says the inspection was the right call.

## 8. The program retrospective

The 8,000-piece throw program for the European hotel group was a successful B2B cashmere program. The hotel opened on time with all 8,000 throws in the suites and the premium rooms. The 6 colorways hit the Pantone TCX targets within ΔE 1.0 (a tighter target than the spec required). The construction met the hand-feel and drape expectations. The packaging was a brand asset for the property, not just a logistics solution.

The program was also a learning experience for us. We learned that the 14-month active period was tight for an 8,000-piece custom program, and that the in-person QC inspection was the highest-leverage quality investment we made. We will use these lessons in the 2027 programs we are already pre-ordering.

If you are planning a similar program — mid-volume (3,000-15,000 pieces), custom colorways, multiple sizes, tight timeline — the lessons from this case study apply directly. The most important ones are:

- The sample phase is the highest-leverage 8 weeks in the program. Do not skip it.
- The in-person QC inspection is the most cost-effective QC investment. Do not skip it.
- The design changes are expensive. Push them to the start of the program, not the middle.
- The packaging is a real cost. Include it in the budget from the start.
- The custom colorways are the biggest single line item. Consider a standing dye-lot program for 50-70% of the colors and custom for the remainder.

For a 30-60 minute conversation about your own program, we are happy to walk through the structure, the milestones, the cost lines, and the lessons. Our sample room calendar for 2027 program development is open; the typical timeline is 3 months from initial brief to a locked specification, and 12-16 months from initial brief to first delivery for an 8,000-piece program.

### Cashmere Authentication: A B2B Buyer's Field Guide to Verifying 100% Cashmere at Receiving

*Published 2026-10-15*

How a B2B buyer verifies that a cashmere shipment is actually 100% cashmere — burn test, microscope, chemical, hand-feel, micron, and weight test methods, with what each one catches and what each one misses. Written for the wholesale receiving team.

# Cashmere Authentication: A B2B Buyer's Field Guide to Verifying 100% Cashmere at Receiving

The single most common fraud in the cashmere industry in 2026 is the 100% cashmere claim that is actually a blend. The blend is usually 70% cashmere / 30% wool — a soft enough blend that the hand-feel is close to 100% cashmere, the price is meaningfully lower (the wool costs roughly 1/8 of cashmere), and the brand can sell it at the 100% cashmere retail price point with a meaningful margin lift. The blend is illegal under most consumer protection laws and the wool industry has been pushing for stronger enforcement, but the reality is that the fraud is widespread enough that a B2B buyer's receiving QC is the only reliable line of defense.

This page is the field guide for the wholesale receiving team. It covers the 6 most common authentication methods, what each one catches, what each one misses, and how to combine them in a 30-minute receiving inspection. The methods are ordered from cheapest and fastest to most expensive and most accurate; the recommended workflow is to run the cheap methods first, escalate to the expensive methods only when the cheap methods give a suspicious signal.

The methods are not proprietary — every QC textbook for protein fibers covers the same set. The difference is doing all 6, in the right order, with the right documentation.

## 1. Method 1: The hand-feel test (free, 30 seconds)

The hand-feel test is the cheapest and the most subjective. A trained grader can tell a 100% cashmere garment from a 70/30 cashmere/wool blend in about 30 seconds, but the training is significant — typically 10+ years of working with cashmere yarn daily. The grader does not need a lab; the grader needs the experience.

What it catches:
- Coarse wool blends (a 50/50 cashmere/wool feels distinctly woolly)
- Synthetic blends (polyester, acrylic — these have a plastic feel)
- Over-processed cashmere (cashmere that has been chemically treated to feel softer than it actually is, which is a sign of a low-grade fiber)

What it misses:
- 70/30 or 80/20 cashmere/wool blends (these are too close to 100% cashmere for hand-feel to reliably detect)
- Cashmere/yak blends (yak is closer to cashmere in hand-feel than wool is)
- Reclaimed cashmere (recycled cashmere fiber, which has been broken down and re-spun, feels different but is still 100% cashmere)

For a B2B receiving team that does not have a trained grader on staff, the hand-feel test is a useful first-pass check. If the hand-feel raises a flag, escalate to Method 2. If the hand-feel is positive, do not conclude that the garment is 100% cashmere — escalate to Method 2 anyway, because the hand-feel is not a definitive test.

## 2. Method 2: The visual inspection (free, 2-3 minutes per piece)

The visual inspection is also free but is more objective than the hand-feel. The 5 things to look for:

**Fiber length.** Cashmere fibers are typically 32-40mm. Reclaimed cashmere is shorter (15-25mm) and more variable. Pull a few fibers from an inconspicuous seam and measure the length. If the length is consistently 32-40mm, the fiber is virgin cashmere. If the length is short or variable, the fiber is reclaimed or blended.

**Fiber diameter distribution.** A true 100% cashmere garment will have a small percentage of guard hairs (the coarse outer fibers that the dehairing process removes imperfectly). The guard hairs are 25-30µm, vs the 14-16µm of the undercoat. The guard hairs are visible as occasional thicker fibers. A blend with wool will have a much higher percentage of thick fibers, and the thick fibers will be more uniform (wool is more uniform in diameter than cashmere guard hairs).

**Color uniformity.** A 100% cashmere garment will have very subtle color variation across the surface (because the natural fiber color is slightly variable). A blend with wool will have more uniform color (because wool is more uniform in dye uptake). This is a subtle signal and a trained grader can detect it; an untrained buyer probably cannot.

**Weave or knit density.** Cashmere is typically woven or knitted at a tighter density than wool blends. The visual density of a 100% cashmere garment is slightly higher than a 70/30 cashmere/wool blend at the same gauge. This is a small signal and a trained grader can detect it.

**Label consistency.** The 100% cashmere label should be consistent with the rest of the garment's labeling. If the brand label says 100% cashmere but the country-of-origin label says something different, that is a red flag.

The visual inspection takes 2-3 minutes per piece. For a 5,000-piece PO, a 2-person team can inspect 100-150 pieces per day. The inspection is worth the time, but it is not a definitive test.

## 3. Method 3: The burn test (free, 5 minutes per fiber sample)

The burn test is the oldest cashmere authentication method. The procedure:

1. Pull 5-10 fibers from an inconspicuous seam.
2. Hold the fibers with tweezers.
3. Light the fibers with a match or lighter.
4. Observe the burn behavior.

What cashmere does when burned:
- Curls away from the flame
- Smells like burning hair (the sulfur in the protein)
- Burns slowly, with a self-extinguishing behavior
- Leaves a black, brittle ash that crushes easily between the fingers

What wool does when burned:
- Curls away from the flame
- Smells like burning hair (wool is also a protein fiber)
- Burns slowly, with a self-extinguishing behavior
- Leaves a black, brittle ash that crushes easily between the fingers

What cashmere and wool have in common: the burn behavior is identical. The burn test cannot distinguish cashmere from wool.

What synthetic fibers do when burned:
- Melts (does not burn)
- Smells like plastic or chemicals
- Leaves a hard, plastic bead

The burn test catches synthetic blends. It does not catch wool blends. So the burn test is useful for ruling out polyester / acrylic / nylon blends, but it is not useful for the 70/30 cashmere/wool fraud that is the most common in 2026.

For the burn test, the procedure takes 5 minutes per fiber sample. A receiving team can run 10-20 samples per hour. If a sample burns with a plastic smell, escalate to Method 4 immediately. If a sample burns like a protein fiber, escalate to Method 4 anyway, because the burn test does not rule out wool blends.

## 4. Method 4: The microscope test (~$50, 10 minutes per fiber sample)

The microscope test is the cheapest laboratory method. A 100x to 400x stereo microscope is sufficient. The procedure:

1. Mount 5-10 fibers on a glass slide.
2. Examine under 100x magnification.
3. Observe the fiber surface.

What cashmere fibers look like under the microscope:
- Smooth, with very fine surface scales (the cuticle)
- The scales are barely visible at 100x, more visible at 400x
- The fibers are slightly variable in diameter along their length (cashmere is a natural fiber with subtle diameter variation)

What wool fibers look like under the microscope:
- Larger, more pronounced surface scales
- The scales are clearly visible at 100x
- The fibers are more uniform in diameter

What synthetic fibers look like under the microscope:
- Smooth, with no surface scales
- The fibers are perfectly uniform in diameter
- Often have a characteristic shape (round, trilobal, etc.)

The microscope test catches wool blends and synthetic blends. It does not catch yak blends (yak is similar to cashmere in surface scale structure). The microscope test takes 10 minutes per fiber sample, plus the cost of the microscope (a used 100x stereo microscope can be purchased for $50-200). For a B2B receiving team, a 100x stereo microscope is a reasonable investment.

If the microscope test raises a flag, escalate to Method 5. If the microscope test is positive (the fibers look like cashmere), escalate to Method 5 anyway, because the microscope does not rule out yak blends and does not give a quantitative measurement.

## 5. Method 5: The chemical dissolution test ($150-300 per sample, 2-3 days)

The chemical dissolution test is the standard ISO method for fiber identification. The procedure:

1. Take a small fiber sample (typically 1-2g).
2. Dissolve the sample in a series of solvents (acetone, then sulfuric acid, then sodium hypochlorite).
3. Each solvent dissolves a specific fiber type and not others.
4. The remaining fiber after each dissolution is weighed, giving a quantitative breakdown of the fiber composition.

The chemical dissolution test catches all common blends: wool, yak, synthetic, and any combination. It is the most reliable test in this list, and the one that B2B buyers should use for the first PO from a new mill and for any PO where the hand-feel or microscope test raises a flag.

The cost is $150-300 per sample, and the turnaround is 2-3 business days at an ISO 17025 lab. For a B2B receiving team, the standard practice is:

- 1 sample per colorway per size for any PO above $5,000
- 1 sample per dye lot for any PO above $20,000
- 1 sample per production batch for any PO above $50,000

For the 8,000-piece hotel case study referenced in our 2026 program retrospective, the chemical dissolution test was run on 12 samples (6 colorways × 2 batches) at $200 per sample = $2,400 total. The 12 samples all came back as 100% cashmere. The $2,400 was a small percentage of the program cost and was the highest-leverage QC investment in the program.

## 6. Method 6: The laser micron test ($150-300 per sample, 2-3 days)

The laser micron test is the quantitative test for fiber diameter. The procedure:

1. Take a small fiber sample (typically 0.5-1g).
2. The lab prepares a fiber snippet and measures the diameter using laser diffraction.
3. The lab reports a mean diameter, a standard deviation, and a distribution.

For 100% cashmere, the expected mean is 14-16.5µm with a standard deviation under 4µm. Anything outside this range is a red flag.

The laser micron test catches most blends (wool is typically 20-25µm, yak is 16-19µm, synthetic is variable but usually not in the cashmere range). It is the most quantitative method, and the one that B2B buyers should use for any program that is targeting the premium cashmere market (where the 14-15.5µm grade is the standard).

The cost is $150-300 per sample, and the turnaround is 2-3 business days. For a B2B receiving team, the standard practice is to combine the chemical dissolution test and the laser micron test into a single QC submission. Most ISO 17025 labs offer both tests, and the combined cost is $250-450 per sample with a 3-5 business day turnaround.

## 7. The recommended receiving workflow

For a B2B cashmere receiving team, the recommended workflow is:

1. **Hand-feel test on 10% of the shipment.** If a single piece raises a flag, escalate that piece to Method 2.
2. **Visual inspection on the 10% sample.** If a single piece raises a flag, escalate that piece to Method 3.
3. **Burn test on 1% of the shipment.** If a single sample burns with a plastic smell, escalate to Method 5 (chemical dissolution) to confirm the synthetic content.
4. **Microscope test on 1% of the shipment.** If a single sample shows clear wool scales, escalate to Method 5.
5. **Chemical dissolution + laser micron on 1 sample per colorway per size.** This is the definitive test; if the first 1-2 samples pass, the rest of the lot is likely fine.

The total cost of this workflow, for a 5,000-piece PO with 6 colorways and 4 sizes, is:

- Hand-feel: 30 minutes per receiving specialist × 2 specialists × 0.5 days = 1 person-day. Cost: $200-400 in labor.
- Visual: 2-3 minutes per piece × 500 pieces = 16-25 hours. Cost: $400-600 in labor.
- Burn: 5 minutes per sample × 50 samples = 4 hours. Cost: $100-200 in labor.
- Microscope: 10 minutes per sample × 50 samples = 8 hours. Cost: $200-400 in labor.
- Chemical dissolution + laser micron: $300-450 per sample × 24 samples = $7,200-10,800.

Total: roughly $8,200-12,400 per 5,000-piece PO. This is 1-2% of the typical PO value, and it is the most cost-effective QC investment a B2B cashmere buyer can make.

## 8. The documentation that should accompany every test

For every test result, the B2B receiving team should keep a documentation record that includes:

- The lot number and dye lot
- The colorway
- The size
- The piece number (if a specific piece was tested)
- The test method
- The test result
- The lab name and certification number
- The test date

This documentation is the QC traceability chain that the brand can show to a consumer, a regulator, or a customs broker. It is also the documentation that the brand can use to escalate a quality issue to the mill, with the test results as the basis for the conversation.

The documentation should be kept for at least 5 years (the typical consumer warranty window for cashmere garments). For programs with longer warranties (some European luxury brands offer 10-year warranties), the documentation should be kept for the warranty period.

## 9. What the test results actually mean

For a 100% cashmere claim, the expected test results are:

- Hand-feel: soft, with no woolly or plastic feel
- Visual: subtle color variation, occasional guard hairs, tight density
- Burn: protein fiber burn (smells like hair, self-extinguishing, black brittle ash)
- Microscope: smooth surface with fine scales
- Chemical dissolution: 100% cashmere (no residual fiber after the cashmere-specific dissolution)
- Laser micron: 14-16.5µm mean, <4µm standard deviation

For a 70/30 cashmere/wool blend:

- Hand-feel: slightly woolly, with reduced softness
- Visual: more uniform color, more uniform fiber diameter, less density
- Burn: protein fiber burn (cannot distinguish)
- Microscope: clear wool scales
- Chemical dissolution: ~70% cashmere, ~30% wool
- Laser micron: 17-22µm mean (the wool pulls the average up)

For a 50/50 cashmere/wool blend:

- Hand-feel: distinctly woolly
- Visual: very uniform, very dense wool appearance
- Burn: protein fiber burn
- Microscope: very clear wool scales
- Chemical dissolution: ~50% cashmere, ~50% wool
- Laser micron: 19-24µm mean

For a synthetic blend (e.g. 70% cashmere / 30% polyester):

- Hand-feel: plastic or synthetic feel
- Visual: very uniform, sometimes with a sheen
- Burn: melts, smells like plastic, leaves a hard bead
- Microscope: smooth, perfectly uniform diameter
- Chemical dissolution: ~70% cashmere, ~30% synthetic
- Laser micron: 14-18µm mean (synthetic fiber can be made at any diameter)

For a yak blend (e.g. 80% cashmere / 20% yak):

- Hand-feel: close to 100% cashmere
- Visual: subtle differences only
- Burn: protein fiber burn
- Microscope: close to cashmere
- Chemical dissolution: 80% cashmere, 20% yak
- Laser micron: 15-17µm mean (yak is slightly thicker than cashmere)

## 10. The escalation protocol

If any of the 6 tests gives a suspicious signal, the escalation protocol is:

1. **Confirm with a second test.** Run the same test on a different sample from the same piece, or a different piece from the same lot. If the second test confirms the first, escalate.
2. **Run Method 5 or 6.** The chemical dissolution test and the laser micron test are the definitive tests. Run one or both.
3. **Quarantine the lot.** The lot should be held in a separate warehouse area, not mixed with the passing inventory. The cost of the quarantine is the cost of a few days of warehouse space.
4. **Contact the mill.** Provide the test results and the documentation. The mill's response window is typically 5-7 business days for an investigation, and 14-30 days for a resolution.
5. **Resolve.** The resolution is typically one of: a re-do of the lot at the mill's cost, a credit for the lot, or a renegotiation of the price. The brand should not accept a "the test is wrong" response — the mill's response should be based on the mill's own testing of the same lot.

The escalation protocol is slow. A typical escalation takes 30-45 days from the first suspicious signal to the resolution. This is why the receiving workflow matters — the first 4 methods (hand-feel, visual, burn, microscope) are all done at the receiving warehouse, and the suspicious signal is caught within 1-2 days of the lot arrival. The lab tests (chemical dissolution, laser micron) take 2-3 business days, and the mill's investigation takes 5-7 business days. The total is 8-12 days for a fast escalation, or 30-45 days for a full escalation with a re-do or a credit.

## 11. The 5 takeaways

For a B2B cashmere receiving team, the 5 takeaways from this field guide:

**1. The hand-feel and visual tests are not enough.** They catch obvious blends, but not the 70/30 cashmere/wool fraud that is the most common in 2026. The chemical dissolution test is the only reliable test for the 70/30 blend.

**2. The burn test catches synthetic blends but not wool blends.** Do not use the burn test as a definitive test. It is a useful first-pass test for synthetic content, but it does not replace the chemical dissolution test.

**3. The microscope test is a useful first-pass test for wool blends.** It catches obvious wool blends, but not the 70/30 blend. Escalate to the chemical dissolution test if the microscope is suspicious.

**4. The chemical dissolution test and the laser micron test are the definitive tests.** A B2B receiving team should run both, on 1 sample per colorway per size, for any PO above $5,000.

**5. The QC cost is 1-2% of the PO value.** The 1-2% is the most cost-effective insurance a B2B cashmere buyer can buy. Skipping the QC is a false economy.

For a 30-60 minute conversation about your own receiving QC program, we are happy to walk through the test methods, the cost, and the documentation. The recommended workflow for a 5,000-piece program is $8,000-12,000 in QC cost, which is roughly 1-2% of the typical PO value.

### Cashmere Maintenance & Storage Guide for B2B Buyers: Pre-Retail Care, Long-Haul Shipping, and After-Sale Support

*Published 2026-10-15*

A 2026 B2B buyer's maintenance guide: how to receive cashmere from your Ordos factory, store it before retail, ship it to your customers, and handle the after-sale care questions. Written for the wholesale buyer, not the end consumer.

# Cashmere Maintenance & Storage Guide for B2B Buyers: Pre-Retail Care, Long-Haul Shipping, and After-Sale Support

The cashmere maintenance questions that come up most often in 2026 are not the end-consumer care questions — those are well-covered by every cashmere brand's care card. The questions that come up are the wholesale buyer's: how do I store the cashmere when it arrives from the Ordos mill, how do I ship it to my retail customer, and how do I handle the after-sale support questions that flow back to me from the end consumer.

This page is the wholesale version of the cashmere care guide. It covers pre-retail storage at the brand warehouse, long-haul shipping to retail customers, the after-sale support questions, and the inventory management issues that distinguish a cashmere program from a wool or cotton program. None of it is a replacement for the end-consumer care card — for that, see the 2026 Winter Cashmere Care Guide. This is the upstream version that the wholesale buyer needs to know.

## 1. The pre-retail storage window

The typical wholesale cashmere program has a 30-90 day pre-retail storage window: the mill ships the bulk production, the brand warehouse receives it, the brand inspects and packs, and the orders are fulfilled to retail customers or store locations. This is the period where cashmere is most vulnerable to the four main storage risks: humidity, moth, compression, and light.

**Humidity.** Cashmere fiber is hygroscopic — it absorbs and releases moisture from the surrounding air. The ideal storage humidity for cashmere is 50-55% relative humidity. Below 40%, the fiber dries out and becomes brittle. Above 60%, the fiber absorbs too much moisture and is at risk of mildew. The damage is not visible immediately; a cashmere sweater stored at 75% humidity for 60 days will show the mildew in 6-12 months when the customer wears it.

The fix: climate-controlled warehouse. If your warehouse is in a humid climate (Southeast US, southern Japan, Mediterranean, southern China), the air conditioning should be on, and you should have a dehumidifier in the cashmere storage area. If your warehouse is in a dry climate (US Mountain West, northern China, central Europe), the heating should be on, and you should have a humidifier in the cashmere storage area. The humidity monitor is the cheapest insurance you can buy.

**Moth.** Cashmere is a protein fiber, and clothes moths (Tineola bisselliella) and carpet beetles (Dermestidae) eat protein fibers. The moth is the bigger risk because the larva can eat through a cashmere garment in 2-3 weeks if left undisturbed. The fix: cedar blocks or lavender sachets in the storage area (NOT mothballs — the smell is permanent and toxic). The more robust fix: sealed plastic bins with a few drops of cedar oil. The most robust fix: a professional pest-control contract that includes quarterly inspections.

**Compression.** Cashmere garments stored under heavy weight (such as stacked under other inventory) can develop permanent compression marks. The marks are usually recoverable with a steam press, but the recovery is not 100%. The fix: store cashmere on hangers (for sweaters and cardigans) or flat-folded with acid-free tissue between layers (for scarves and blankets). For bulk storage in cardboard boxes, line the box with acid-free tissue and limit the stack to 5 garments.

**Light.** Direct sunlight fades cashmere color over 4-6 weeks. The fix: store cashmere in opaque boxes or in a dark corner of the warehouse. Most brands use opaque cotton garment bags for in-warehouse storage; the bags protect from dust, light, and minor compression.

The 30-90 day pre-retail window is not a long time. With reasonable storage conditions, cashmere is stable. The risk increases if the window stretches to 6+ months — at that point, even good storage conditions start to show some fiber degradation.

## 2. Receiving cashmere from the mill

When the mill ships the cashmere (typically by ocean freight in a corrugated cardboard carton, vacuum-packed or polybagged), the receiving process at the brand warehouse should follow a 5-step protocol. We provide this protocol to all wholesale clients.

**Step 1: Inspect the carton condition before opening.** Look for water damage, puncture, or unusual weight. If the carton has visible water damage, photograph it before opening (for the shipping insurance claim) and open in a clean area to assess the garment damage.

**Step 2: Open in a clean area and count units.** Confirm the unit count against the packing list. If there is a discrepancy, document immediately.

**Step 3: Visual inspection of each unit.** Look for stains, holes, color inconsistencies, and sizing inconsistencies. If a unit has any of these, set it aside for the QC team to evaluate. Most reputable mills have an allowance of 1-3% for visible defects; the defect rate above 5% is a conversation with the mill.

**Step 4: Random QC inspection.** Pull 5-10% of the units and inspect them against the original spec. For a 5,000-piece PO, inspect 250-500 pieces. The random sample should match the original sample (lab dip for color, first 5 pieces for silhouette and gauge). If the random sample does not match, the rest of the lot is suspect.

**Step 5: Storage decision.** If the lot passes inspection, store per the conditions in section 1. If it does not, quarantine the lot and open a QC conversation with the mill within 48 hours. The mill's response window is typically 5-7 business days for an investigation; the resolution window is 14-30 days for a re-do or a credit.

The 5-step protocol takes about 4-6 hours per 1,000 pieces for a warehouse team of 2-3 people. The investment in the protocol pays off in lower defect rates at retail, lower return rates from end consumers, and a faster QC loop with the mill.

## 3. Long-haul shipping to retail

Once the cashmere is in the brand warehouse and the orders are being fulfilled, the shipping question becomes relevant. The two main shipping modes are ocean freight (3-6 weeks) and air freight (3-7 days). Both have specific cashmere considerations.

**Ocean freight.** The standard mode for cashmere wholesale shipments from Ordos to retail warehouses in North America, Europe, or Japan. The key consideration is moisture control. A standard 40-foot shipping container experiences temperature swings of 10-30°C during a trans-Pacific transit, with humidity swings of 40-90%. The humidity swing is the bigger risk — at 90% humidity for 30 days, the cashmere can develop the start of mildew that does not show until 6-12 months later.

The fix: desiccant bags in each shipping carton. The standard practice is 4-6 desiccant bags (50g silica gel) per 12-piece carton. The bags absorb the humidity spikes during transit. Cost is roughly $0.10-0.30 per garment; the cost is trivial compared to the risk.

**Air freight.** Used for reorders, late deliveries, and small-lot programs. The transit time is 3-7 days, which means the humidity exposure is much shorter. The main risk with air freight is compression — air freight tends to use heavier cartons with more aggressive stacking, and the compression marks on a cashmere garment are visible at retail.

The fix: ask the freight forwarder for "soft stack" or "no double-stack" handling. The cost premium is $50-150 per shipment; the result is fewer compression-mark issues at retail.

For both modes, the brand warehouse should do an incoming inspection on the cashmere as soon as the cartons arrive. The 5-step protocol from section 2 applies, with the additional check that the desiccant bags are still dry (they should be — if they are saturated, the transit conditions were worse than expected).

## 4. The after-sale support questions

The 8 most common after-sale support questions that flow back to wholesale buyers from end consumers in 2026, in roughly the order of frequency:

**Q1: "How do I wash this?"** Answer: cold water (20°C or below), pH-neutral wool wash, hand wash or delicate cycle in a mesh laundry bag, lay flat to dry. The end-consumer care card should cover this. If the care card is missing, redirect to the brand's standard care guidance, not to the mill.

**Q2: "Is this real cashmere?"** Answer: yes, with the OEKO-TEX or other certification number on the care label. If the buyer needs to verify, the mill can provide a 100g fiber sample from the same lot for comparison (this is unusual but happens for high-end resellers).

**Q3: "Why is it pilling?"** Answer: pilling in the first 2-4 wears is normal and is a function of loose surface fibers. After 5-6 wears, pilling should reduce with a cashmere comb. Persistent pilling beyond 5-6 wears may indicate a yarn quality issue, in which case the brand should investigate with the mill.

**Q4: "The color is fading."** Answer: most natural-fiber dyes have a 1-2% color shift in the first 5 washes. If the fading is dramatic, it may be an issue with the dye lot or the wash water (chlorine, hard water, hot water). The brand should ask the consumer to provide a photo of the original color and the faded color to assess.

**Q5: "There's a hole in it."** Answer: a hole is either a moth damage (consumer-side issue), a manufacturing defect (mill-side issue), or a wear-through from friction (consumer-side issue). The brand's QC team should look at the photo and the lot history to determine the source.

**Q6: "Can I dry clean it?"** Answer: yes, but with restrictions. Standard dry cleaning is fine for cashmere. Trichloroethylene-based dry cleaning is fine. Perchloroethylene-based dry cleaning is the industry standard and is fine. Wet cleaning is also fine if the cleaner has cashmere experience. The most common dry-cleaning damage to cashmere is over-pressing, which flattens the fiber and reduces softness.

**Q7: "How do I store it in summer?"** Answer: clean before storage, fold (don't hang), store in breathable cotton (not plastic), add cedar or lavender, store in a dark closet. This is the "summer storage" question that comes up every spring.

**Q8: "What if it shrinks?"** Answer: cashmere shrinks when washed in hot water or dried in a dryer. If the consumer did this, the shrinkage is permanent and there is no recovery. If the consumer did not, the shrinkage is likely a manufacturing issue (yarn was over-twisted or finished at too high a temperature) and the brand should investigate with the mill.

For Q3, Q4, Q5, and Q8, the wholesale buyer's role is to be the bridge between the consumer and the mill. The mill can provide a 100g fiber sample from the same lot for the consumer to compare, or a defect analysis from the same lot to determine the likely cause. The wholesale buyer's role is to make the handoff smoothly and to track the cases so that patterns (e.g. 5% of units in a particular lot have an issue) get caught early.

## 5. Inventory management for cashmere

Cashmere inventory management is different from wool or cotton inventory management for three reasons:

**Cashmere is a high-value, low-volume item.** A typical B2B cashmere program is 5,000-50,000 pieces per year. A typical B2B cotton program is 100,000-500,000 pieces per year. The cashmere program needs more careful unit-level tracking because the per-piece cost is higher and the impact of an inventory error is larger.

**Cashmere has a longer design-to-shelf cycle.** A cashmere program that ships in Q3 2027 needs design and PO in Q4 2026, with sample room iterations in Q2-Q3 2026. A cotton program that ships in Q3 2027 needs design in Q1 2027, with sample room iterations in Q1 2027. The cashmere program needs longer forecasting windows.

**Cashmere has higher replacement costs.** If a cashmere garment is damaged in the warehouse (moth, mildew, compression, color shift), the brand has to either repair the garment (which is expensive — $10-20 per piece for a quality repair) or replace it from the mill (which has a 30-45 day lead time). If a cotton garment is damaged, the brand can replace it from a local supplier in 2-3 weeks at a fraction of the cost.

The practical implication: cashmere programs need better inventory visibility than cotton or wool programs. The wholesale buyer should have:

- A unit-level inventory system (not just SKU-level) so that damaged units can be tracked back to the lot, the mill, the dye lot, the production period.
- A FIFO (first in, first out) rotation system for the cashmere inventory so that older stock goes out first.
- A 60-day inventory health check for any cashmere in the warehouse for more than 90 days. The check is visual inspection + 5-piece lab test for color shift.
- A pre-allocated replacement budget for damaged units. The typical budget is 3-5% of the cashmere inventory value.

For a brand that is not yet doing these four things, the cost of cashmere inventory management is higher than the cost of doing it. The break-even on a unit-level inventory system is usually 1-2 seasons of cashmere inventory.

## 6. The seasonal calendar for cashmere

Cashmere has a predictable seasonal calendar for wholesale buyers. Understanding the calendar helps with inventory planning and consumer messaging.

**Q1 (Jan-Mar):** FW delivery season. The fall/winter collection ships to retail. The wholesale buyer's job is to manage the inventory ramp-down of FW stock and the inventory ramp-up of SS stock.

**Q2 (Apr-Jun):** SS delivery season. The spring/summer collection ships to retail. The wholesale buyer's job is to manage the SS inventory and the end-of-FW markdown season. The Q2 is also the period for the consumer to ask the summer storage questions — see Q7 in section 4.

**Q3 (Jul-Sep):** FW development season. The fall/winter program is being designed, sampled, and approved. The wholesale buyer's job is to coordinate with the mill on the sample room and the pre-order. This is also the consumer to ask the "how do I store my cashmere" question, which the wholesale buyer should have a standard answer for.

**Q4 (Oct-Dec):** FW pre-order season. The fall/winter program is being placed as a PO. The wholesale buyer's job is to confirm the pre-order with the mill, finalize the production calendar, and prepare for the Q1 FW delivery. The Q4 is also the holiday gifting season — cashmere is a high-end gift, and the brand's holiday messaging should highlight the cashmere program.

The seasonal calendar is predictable enough that a wholesale buyer can plan the inventory and the consumer messaging 12 months in advance. The risk is in the Q3-Q4 transition, when the new FW program is being designed and the old FW inventory is being cleared. This is the period when a brand's cashmere program can get out of sync with the consumer demand.

## 7. The B2B buyer's monthly checklist

A practical checklist for the wholesale buyer, by month:

- **Jan:** FW sell-through review; reorder analysis; consumer feedback summary.
- **Feb:** FW markdown planning; SS pre-development.
- **Mar:** SS sample room; FW replacement orders; pre-FW year-end plan.
- **Apr:** SS sample room; FW closeout; SS pre-orders.
- **May:** SS PO confirm; consumer summer storage content; moth-prevention prep.
- **Jun:** SS pre-orders close; SS sample room; mid-year QC review.
- **Jul:** SS sell-in; FW sample room; SS replacement orders.
- **Aug:** FW sample room; SS sell-through; pre-FW consumer content.
- **Sep:** FW pre-orders; SS markdown; FW sample room.
- **Oct:** FW pre-orders close; holiday gift prep; FW production calendar.
- **Nov:** FW production start; SS closeout; holiday sell-through.
- **Dec:** FW production; year-end review; SS development plan.

The checklist is not exhaustive — every brand will have variations. But it captures the rhythm of a cashmere B2B program, and it is the kind of calendar that separates a stable cashmere program from one that has inventory surprises every season.

## 8. The support infrastructure we provide

For our wholesale clients, we provide a small support infrastructure that reduces the after-sale support questions and the inventory management overhead:

- **Pre-emptive care cards in 6 languages.** We provide the care card design files (PDF and SVG) in our 6 supported languages. The brand can print them on the care label or include them as a separate card with each garment.
- **Inventory check service.** For wholesale clients with framework agreements, we run an annual inventory check on any cashmere older than 12 months. The check is visual inspection + lab test for color shift. The cost is on us.
- **Pre-emptive defect tracking.** For any PO above $5,000, we maintain a defect log that the wholesale buyer can request. The log is updated quarterly with any defect rate changes, color issues, or sizing issues that we see across the production batches.

These three services are part of our standard wholesale relationship. For buyers who want to develop a more comprehensive support infrastructure, we have a recommended partner network of cashmere-specific repair services (in 4 locations: US East Coast, US West Coast, EU, and Japan) that can handle mending, re-knitting, and color restoration for end-consumer returns.

The after-sale support question is the single biggest contributor to consumer loyalty in a cashmere program. A brand that handles the support well is a brand that gets repeat orders. A brand that handles the support poorly is a brand that loses to the next B2B cashmere program that does it better.

### 2026 Cashmere Supply Chain Risk: How B2B Buyers Vet Their Ordos Mill

*Published 2026-10-15*

A practical B2B buyer's guide to evaluating a cashmere supplier's supply chain — herd sourcing, dehairing capacity, processing controls, and the documentation that proves each step. Written from an Ordos factory's perspective on what buyers actually verify.

# 2026 Cashmere Supply Chain Risk: How B2B Buyers Vet Their Ordos Mill

The most expensive lesson in cashmere sourcing in 2026 is the same one buyers have been learning for the last decade: a cashmere sweater at a unit price that is 30% below comparable offers is rarely a bargain. It is usually a supply chain problem you cannot see from the price quote — wrong fiber, wrong origin, wrong dehairing, wrong yarn count, or all four. The fix is a structured supply chain evaluation before the first PO, not a complaint letter after the third rejection.

This page is the supply chain evaluation checklist we walk through with new wholesale clients during their first site visit. It is what an experienced B2B cashmere buyer's QC team would test, in the order they would test it, with the documentation they would request. None of it is proprietary — every item is a known industry standard. The difference is doing all of it, in the right order, with the right person on the supplier side answering.

## 1. The four supply chain risk vectors in cashmere

The cashmere supply chain has four points where quality, cost, and risk diverge. Every cashmere B2B program gets evaluated on the same four vectors, in this order:

**Vector 1: Herd and fiber origin.** Where is the cashmere fiber physically coming from, who owns the goats, who tends them, who shears them, who buys the raw fiber from the herders, and what is the traceback path from your finished garment back to the goat? This is the UFLPA / CBAM / Lacey Act question. The answer is verifiable — it is a paper trail.

**Vector 2: Dehairing and processing controls.** Dehairing is the most expensive step in the fiber preparation (roughly 30-40% of the total cost of a 100% cashmere finished garment), and the step that introduces the most variability in hand, micron consistency, and contamination level. A mill can be honest about its herd sourcing and still produce inconsistent yarn if its dehairing is sloppy. This is the process question.

**Vector 3: Yarn count and gauge honesty.** Yarn count (Nm 2/26, 2/48, 2/60) and stitch density (7gg, 12gg, 14gg) are two of the most-often-misrepresented specs in cashmere contracts. A 12gg garment that is actually 9gg will pass visual inspection at the sample room but fail on every repeat order. This is the spec question.

**Vector 4: Margin structure and risk-sharing.** A mill that quotes at 6% margin on a fixed-quantity PO is a stable business partner. A mill that quotes at 2% margin is one bad PO away from bankruptcy. This is the business question.

Most B2B buyers focus on Vector 1 because that is what the regulation and media attention has put in front of them. The four are not equal — Vector 1 is necessary but not sufficient. A buyer who only audits Vector 1 will get a clean supply chain and a yarn quality problem; a buyer who only audits Vector 3 will get a great-looking first sample and a quality disaster on the second repeat.

## 2. Vector 1: The 8-document traceback checklist

For Vector 1, you need a paper trail that ties your finished garment back to the herder. We provide the following 8 documents for every PO above $5,000. We give them to wholesale clients, brand buyers, and customs brokers on request. Most reputable Ordos mills can produce the same set; if your supplier cannot, that is a yellow flag, not a red flag — but a yellow flag is enough to slow down the relationship.

1. **Certificate of Origin** issued by the local Industry & Commerce Bureau (鄂尔多斯市工商行政管理局) with the Bureau stamp. This is the single most important document for customs. It states the location of dehairing, spinning, and finishing. Not a self-issued factory certificate.
2. **Processing flow declaration** with each manufacturing step and the geographic location where it occurs. UFLPA enforcement specifically looks for this — it should include the dehairing line, the spinning line, the knitting/weaving line, and the finishing line, with addresses.
3. **Traceback summary** for the fiber lots in your shipment. We identify the herder cooperatives (合作社) that supplied the raw cashmere, with their approximate locations and the season of harvest. Inner Mongolia outside of Xinjiang = no UFLPA issue, but CBP wants the paperwork anyway.
4. **Electricity source declaration** for CBAM. Inner Mongolia grid is approximately 65% coal / 35% wind and solar. We provide the Chinese grid emission factor and the verifiable kWh consumption per kg of yarn output. This determines the CBAM certificate cost.
5. **Fur-fiber absence declaration** for shipments to the EU and California. Confirms that no angora or rabbit fiber is blended into the lot. Routine CBP question on small cashmere lots.
6. **OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certificate** for our yarns. Downloadable from the buyer dashboard. Reduces chemical-input questions under UFLPA.
7. **2025 Sedex SMETA 4-pillar audit report** on file. Available on request for buyers above $50K PO volume.
8. **ISO 9001:2015 + BSCI audit certificates**. Also available on request.

If your supplier can produce all 8 within 5 business days of PO confirmation, the documentation is in good shape. If they need 3-4 weeks, the supply chain is not actually traceable in the way the documentation suggests.

## 3. Vector 2: The 3-test processing audit

For Vector 2, the audit is hands-on, not paper-based. We suggest 3 tests that any reputable mill will let you run during a site visit. If they will not, the dehairing has problems they know about.

**Test 1: Micron consistency test.** Take 50g of yarn from 3 different cones of the same lot. Send to an ISO 17025 lab for laser-micron testing. If the average micron is within 0.5µm of the spec and the standard deviation is under 0.4µm, the dehairing is consistent. If the standard deviation is over 0.6µm, the dehairing is mixing fiber grades. The lab cost is roughly $150-300 per sample; we run this in-house before every bulk production release.

**Test 2: Hand-feel test by a qualified grader.** This is the test that experienced cashmere buyers rely on most. A trained grader can tell in 30 seconds whether a yarn is 100% cashmere, a blend, or a sub-grade fiber. The grader does not need a lab — they need 10+ years of working with cashmere yarn daily. Most brand buyers do not have this expertise in-house; if you do not, hire a third-party consultant for the first 2-3 site visits.

**Test 3: Combing pass count.** Dehairing is a multi-pass operation. Cashmere fiber needs 2-3 combing passes to remove the coarse guard hair and the residual lanolin. A single-pass dehairing is what gives cashmere its "itchy" reputation. Ask the mill to walk you through the dehairing line; count the combing stations; confirm the fiber makes 2 or 3 passes. Single-pass is a red flag.

These three tests are not exhaustive — the full site visit checklist is closer to 20 items — but they are the three that catch 80% of the actual problems we see in cashmere.

## 4. Vector 3: The yarn-count verification

For Vector 3, the test is the most objective and the easiest to do. A 2/48 Nm yarn has 48 kilometers of yarn per kilogram of fiber. A 2/26 Nm yarn has 26. If your supplier says they delivered 2/48 but the actual yarn is 2/36, you can prove it in 3 minutes with a wrap reel and a precision scale.

The procedure:

1. Wrap the yarn on a 1-meter wrap reel. Make 100 wraps (= 100 meters).
2. Weigh the 100-meter skein on a precision scale (0.1g resolution).
3. The weight in grams × 10 = the yarn count in Nm (e.g. 4.17g × 10 = 41.7m/g, which means 41.7 kilometers per kilogram, which is 2/41.7 Nm — close to 2/42, not 2/48).
4. Repeat on 5 skeins from 5 different cones of the same lot.
5. If the average count is within 5% of the spec, the yarn is honest. If it is off by 10% or more, the yarn count is wrong.

Buyers who do this test on every first PO from a new mill catch roughly 1 in 4 yarn-count misrepresentations. The misrepresentations are not always intentional — sometimes they are a sourcing-team error or a communication gap between the spinning mill and the finishing mill. But the practical effect on the buyer is the same: a wrong-count yarn produces a wrong-gauge garment.

## 5. Vector 4: The margin conversation

Vector 4 is uncomfortable but necessary. A mill that quotes at 2% margin on a $50,000 fixed-quantity PO has $1,000 of margin to absorb a 3% input cost spike (which is normal in cashmere — micron shortages, currency moves, transport rate changes). A mill that quotes at 6% margin has $3,000 of buffer for the same spike. The difference between a stable supplier and a flaky one is mostly this.

The honest questions to ask:

- What is your margin on this PO? (A good mill will answer this directly. A bad mill will dodge.)
- What is your worst-case annual raw fiber cost volatility, and how much of that do you absorb before renegotiating? (For cashmere, a 20% raw fiber cost swing in a single season is normal.)
- What is your credit line for raw fiber purchases? (The answer indicates the mill's working capital, which is a leading indicator of stability.)
- What is your annual dehairing capacity utilization, and what is the saturation point? (If the mill is at 90% utilization, they have no buffer for emergency orders — and no buffer for your first repeat order either.)

These are uncomfortable questions. The mills that answer them are the ones to buy from. The mills that refuse to answer, or that get visibly uncomfortable, are the ones that will have supply problems at the worst possible moment for you.

## 6. The 6 red flags to walk away from

If any of these 6 come up in the first 2-3 conversations, walk away. The cashmere market in 2026 is competitive enough that there is no reason to take on a supplier with structural risk.

**Red flag 1: "We can do it cheaper if you don't need the OEKO-TEX certificate."** A mill that suggests this is openly telling you that they have a parallel production line that is not OEKO-TEX compliant. The cheaper line is the one you will get.

**Red flag 2: "Our herder cooperative is in Xinjiang."** The first question every B2B buyer should ask. The first answer every B2B mill should give honestly. If the answer is Xinjiang, walk away — the UFLPA exposure is total and your customs broker will not be able to clear the shipment.

**Red flag 3: "We don't need a contract — we can do this on trust."** A mill that wants to skip the contract wants to skip the consequences if quality is bad. A written contract is the only protection B2B buyers have against silent downgrade.

**Red flag 4: "Our minimum order is 30 pcs."** For 100% cashmere, MOQ is constrained by dehairing batch size, which is 50-200kg of fiber. A 30-pc MOQ means the mill is either blending your order into someone else's batch (and you will not get pure cashmere) or they are holding small inventory (and the fiber is old).

**Red flag 5: "We can ship next week."** Cashmere yarn production is 14-21 days for a standard 2/26 Nm at 100kg. Cashmere knitwear is 30-45 days. A "next week" promise means the mill is shipping from inventory, not from a fresh production run, and you do not know what is in the inventory.

**Red flag 6: "We don't have a fixed price list, every order is quoted."** A mill that re-quotes every order is one whose costs are unstable — usually a sign that the mill is buying fiber on spot markets and passing the cost volatility to the buyer. A reputable mill has a quarterly pricing model with 30-60 day forward visibility.

## 7. The first 90 days: a recommended sequence

For a new B2B cashmere relationship, the first 90 days should look like this:

**Days 1-14: Document review.** Get the 8 documents in section 2. Read them. Verify the 6 red flags in section 6. If the mill can produce the documents and clear the red flags, proceed.

**Days 15-30: Sample room visit.** Visit the mill in person. Run the 3 tests in section 3. Ask the 4 questions in section 5. Take your own photos of the dehairing line, the spinning line, the knitting line, the finishing line. Save them for future reference.

**Days 30-60: First PO.** Place a small first PO (we recommend $5,000-15,000 minimum to get meaningful data on repeat performance). The first PO is a learning PO, not a profit PO. The goal is to validate the mill can deliver what they promised.

**Days 60-90: Yarn-count verification and quality audit.** Run the yarn-count verification (section 4) on the delivered goods. Run a hand-feel evaluation. If the first PO passes, place a second PO at 2-3x the size. If the second PO also passes, you have a supplier.

**Months 4-12: Scale.** Once the relationship is established, the typical ramp pattern for a B2B cashmere relationship is 3-5x year-over-year for the first 3 years, then 1.5-2x for years 4-5. This is the typical B2B cycle for an apparel material supplier.

## 8. What we tell buyers who are evaluating us

For buyers who are evaluating us against the checklist in this article: yes, we can produce the 8 documents in section 2 within 5 business days of PO confirmation. Yes, we welcome site visits at the Ordos facility with a 7-day notice. Yes, we will sit in the room while you run the 3 tests in section 3, and we will not interfere with the test results. Yes, the yarn-count verification in section 4 is exactly how we QC our own production batches before release. Yes, our margin structure is in the 6-8% range, with a 30-day forward price on fiber. Yes, the 6 red flags in section 6 do not apply to us.

What we will not do is lower our price to match a competitor who is willing to skip Vector 1 documentation. We have lost POs in 2026 because of that. We have also kept 90%+ of our wholesale customers from 2024-2026 — and that retention rate is the metric that matters.

For a B2B buyer's first conversation with us: send us your specification, your volume, your destination, and your commercial terms. We will reply within 24 hours with a formal quote and the 8 documents. If you want a site visit, our calendar is open 60-90 days out.
