### Inside an Ordos Cashmere Factory: What B2B Buyers Actually See on a Factory Tour

*Published 2026-09-23*

What to expect on an Ordos cashmere factory tour — facility walkthrough, machinery inventory, QC lab, warehouse inspection, owner interview, and the 8 red flags that should make you walk away.

# Inside an Ordos Cashmere Factory: What B2B Buyers Actually See on a Factory Tour

A factory tour is the single highest-ROI hour you can spend before placing a USD 50K+ cashmere order. Email exchanges, sample shipments, and Zoom meetings all help, but walking a facility tells you things no questionnaire reveals: how workers actually behave when the owner isn't looking, whether the dehairing line is calibrated or running 10-year-old settings, whether the warehouse is organized or stuffed floor-to-ceiling. We've hosted 200+ buyers at our Ordos facility over the last decade and walked through 30+ competitor factories as part of industry events. This guide explains what to look for, what questions to ask, and what red flags should send you home.

If you're evaluating a Chinese cashmere supplier for the first time, plan to spend 2-3 days: one full day at the factory, plus 1-2 days visiting fiber suppliers, dye houses, or finishing facilities. The full tour described below fits in one full day with a serious buyer. Most legitimate factories accommodate visits within 2-3 weeks notice — longer lead times or refusal to host are themselves red flags.

## Before You Arrive: What to Request from the Factory

Send this list to the factory 1-2 weeks before your visit. Their willingness to share is itself a signal:

- **Floor plan** — so you know which areas you'll see and which you won't
- **Worker count** (peak season vs. off-season)
- **Machinery list** — brand, model, year of major equipment (dehairing, spinning, knitting)
- **Recent client references** (3-5 brands with permission to share)
- **Audit history** — any SGS, Bureau Veritas, BSCI, or SA8000 audits from the last 3 years
- **Capacity utilization** — percentage of full capacity they're running today (anything below 40% signals weak demand or recent client losses)
- **Sample swatches** of their current fiber, yarn, and finished goods

**Red flag before you arrive**: Factory refuses to share machinery list, capacity utilization, or recent client references. Walk away before booking the flight.

## Hour 1: Office Tour and Owner/Manager Meeting

The first hour sets the tone. You'll typically start in the front office, meet the owner or general manager, and see sample displays of yarn and finished products.

**What to look for**:

- **Owner involvement**: Is the owner actively in the office during your visit, or do they delegate to a sales manager? Owner-involved factories (especially family-owned) typically have better quality control because decisions get made on the floor, not in committee. **Red flag**: Owner is "traveling" but you see their luxury car parked outside. Suggests they're hiding something.
- **Sample organization**: Yarn cones, fabric swatches, and finished garment samples should be organized by yarn count, micron, and season. Chaotic samples suggest chaotic operations.
- **Office staff presence**: 3-5 office staff for a mid-sized factory is normal. An empty office (just you and one sales person) suggests the factory doesn't have the sales or finance depth to manage ongoing B2B relationships.
- **Sample readiness**: Can they pull a stock yarn cone or sample garment from the shelf in 60 seconds? Or do they have to go to the warehouse? Both are fine, but the former signals efficient sample handling.

**Questions to ask**:
- How long have you been operating this facility? (5+ years is normal; <3 years is risky)
- What's your average client retention rate? (70%+ is healthy)
- What's your largest single-client concentration? (Under 30% is healthier)
- Which export markets do you serve? (Diversified = lower risk)
- Can I see your export license and business registration? (Legitimate factories have these)

## Hour 2: Fiber Warehouse and Dehairing Line

The fiber warehouse reveals whether the factory is honestly sourcing what they sell. Then you walk the dehairing line — the critical step that turns raw cashmere (with guard hair contamination) into usable fiber.

**Fiber warehouse**:

- **Fiber bag labels**: Each bag should have a tag with combing station name, harvest date, micron range, and grade. Generic unlabeled bags = unverifiable provenance.
- **Inventory turnover**: Are new fiber arrivals mixed with old stock (suggesting slow turnover and aging fiber)? Or is there a clear rotation?
- **Storage conditions**: Fiber should be in a dry, ventilated space. Humid or musty storage degrades fiber over time.

**Dehairing line**:

- **Equipment**: Look for make and model nameplates. Italian-made (Carding Machine Services, Cormatex) or quality Chinese (Shanghai Johnny, Shenyang Textile Machinery) dehairing machines are standard. Very old machines or homemade equipment signal cost-cutting.
- **Worker skill**: Workers should be feeding fiber at a controlled rate, not rushing. Quick tension changes or fiber jams mean the line is being pushed past its capacity.
- **Output quality**: The dehaired fiber coming off the line should look clean, uniformly fine, and free of guard hair. Visible guard hair means poor calibration.
- **Dust and noise**: Dehairing generates dust and noise. Some dust is normal; visible clouds of dust in the air mean inadequate ventilation and worker safety risk.

**Red flag**: The factory has only one dehairing line. Most mid-sized factories need 2-3 dehairing lines to handle volume. A single line limits capacity and creates a single point of failure.

## Hour 3: Spinning and Yarn Production

Not every cashmere factory spins its own yarn — many buy yarn from regional spinners. Either approach is legitimate, but the answers to your questions differ.

**If the factory spins yarn in-house**:

- **Spinning frames**: Look for Italian (Gaudino, Savio), German (Zinser), or quality Chinese (Tongxiang) frames. Older mechanical frames (< 1990s) signal aging capacity.
- **Yarn cone storage**: Yarn cones should be stored by count, lot, and color in organized bins. Mixed storage means quality control problems.
- **Lot traceability**: Each cone should trace to a fiber lot, spinning run, and QC record. If they can't trace a cone back to its origin fiber in 60 seconds, their lot control is weak.

**If the factory buys yarn externally**:

- **Yarn supplier relationships**: Ask which spinning mills they source from. Three quality mills (e.g., ERDOS Group's spinning division, Hubei Chunfeng, Zhejiang Xinao) is normal. If they can't name a specific mill, they may be buying from low-quality sources.

**Red flag**: Factory claims to spin in-house but can't show spinning equipment, or claims "directly from fiber to yarn" with no intermediate steps. This is usually a sign they're reselling yarn from another spinner and adding markup.

## Hour 4: Knitting Floor and Cut-and-Sew

This is where most production capacity and labor risk lives. Plan to spend at least 45 minutes here.

**Knitting floor**:

- **Machine count**: 10-30 machines for a mid-sized factory is normal. Fewer than 8 means limited capacity.
- **Machine brands**: STOLL (Germany), Shima Seiki (Japan), Protti (Germany) are premium. Chinese brands (Longxing, Wuxi) are acceptable for stockinette.
- **Machine age and maintenance**: Look for oil stains, rust, broken needles. Well-maintained machines look clean and busy.
- **Operator skill**: Workers should sit at machines with finished garments beside them, not running back and forth to a supervisor.

**Cut-and-sew workshop**:

- **Worker spacing**: Workers should have minimum 1.2 m² each (Chinese labor law). Crowded workshops = quality risk + labor compliance risk.
- **Lighting and ventilation**: Adequate lighting (essential for color matching and stitch inspection). Visible ventilation fans or HVAC.
- **Fire safety**: Fire extinguishers at intervals, emergency exits clearly marked, no blocked exits. Missing = compliance failure.
- **Worker age and demeanor**: No visible child workers. Workers should look alert, not exhausted.

**Red flag**: All sewing machines are old mechanical models (vs. modern servo-controlled). The factory is producing at the lowest end of the quality spectrum — fine for fast fashion, not for premium cashmere.

## Hour 5: Quality Control Lab and Warehouse

The QC lab determines whether the factory can verify its own claims about fiber grade, yarn quality, and garment durability.

**What should be in a serious QC lab**:

- **Fiber diameter analyzer** (OFDA or similar) — measures fiber diameter distribution. Without this, the factory can't validate its 14.5μm claims.
- **Pilling tester** (Martindale or ICI) — simulates wear cycles to test pilling. Critical for cashmere garments.
- **Color fastness testing** — wash, light, and rub fastness.
- **Hand-feel reference samples** — yarn and fabric samples organized by quality grade.
- **Calibration records** — equipment should have current calibration stickers (typically annual calibration).

**Warehouse**:

- **Organization**: Yarn, fabric, and finished goods stored in distinct zones with clear labeling. Mix of unlabeled cartons, half-empty pallets, and crowded floors = poor inventory management.
- **Finished goods age**: Look at the date codes on cartons. If you see cartons from 2023 in a busy factory, either inventory is moving slowly (slow sales) or it's old stock being relabeled (red flag for old product resold as new).
- **Pest control**: Cashmere attracts moths and silverfish. Look for pest control evidence (traps, sealed storage, no visible damage to fiber bags).

**Red flag**: No QC lab visible, or lab equipment looks 15+ years old and uncalibrated. Factory can't validate its own quality claims.

## Hour 6: Lunch, Owner Q&A, and Closing Discussion

Most factory tours wrap up with a working lunch in the factory canteen or a nearby restaurant. This is your chance for a more candid conversation with the owner or GM.

**What to evaluate**:

- **Canteen quality**: Worker food quality signals how the owner treats their workforce. A clean canteen with hot food = decent labor practices. No canteen (workers eat off-site) = possible cost-cutting.
- **Owner transparency**: Does the owner answer questions directly, or deflect to "let me check with my team"? Good owners answer even uncomfortable questions (e.g., "What's your defect rate?" — should be under 3% for finished garments).
- **Worker interviews**: If you have time and language support, interview 2-3 workers (anonymously) about hours, pay, and treatment. Long hours or complaints about wage delays = red flags.

**Questions to wrap up with**:

- Can I see your defect/return rate over the last 12 months? (Healthy factories share this; defensive factories won't)
- What's your on-time delivery rate for the last 12 months? (Should be 90%+ for finished goods)
- Who are your top 3 competitors and why should I work with you instead?
- What's your biggest customer pain point and how are you addressing it?

The answers to these last questions reveal more than 10 hours of facility walkthrough. A factory with 95% on-time delivery, 2% defect rate, and a clear competitive story is worth following up with a sample order. A factory that hedges every question is not.

## Eight Red Flags That Should Make You Walk Away

After 200+ factory visits, these are the eight red flags that, taken together or alone, suggest the factory is not a serious supplier:

1. **Owner not present and refuses to commit a meeting time during your visit**. Either they're avoiding you or they don't care enough to make the time.

2. **Refusal to walk certain areas** ("warehouse is too messy right now" or "we're not allowed"). Legitimate factories have nothing to hide in areas that affect quality.

3. **No fiber traceability documentation**. Bag labels are absent or generic. You can't verify where their cashmere actually came from.

4. **Machinery is 15+ years old across the board**. They're running on depreciated equipment and may not have the cash flow to invest in upgrades.

5. **Single dehairing line**. Capacity is limited, and you have no fallback if it breaks down during your production run.

6. **No QC lab or visibly uncalibrated equipment**. They can't validate the quality they claim.

7. **Worker conditions fail basic inspection** (crowded, blocked exits, no fire safety). Compliance audit failure is a near-certainty for your downstream brand.

8. **Owner or sales staff deflects every direct question**. Vague answers about defect rates, delivery performance, or client retention signal they're hiding something.

One red flag is forgivable. Two warrants a follow-up investigation. Three or more — walk away.

## Virtual Factory Tour: When You Can't Travel

If a China trip isn't feasible (cost, visa, time), request a virtual tour. Most legitimate factories accommodate this within 2-3 days notice. What to ask for:

- **Live video walk-through** via WhatsApp or Zoom — 30-45 minutes, with you asking questions in real time. The factory should walk you through the same 6-hour tour described above, condensed.
- **Worker count visible on camera**: If the "factory" shows 5 workers total, it's not a real factory.
- **Equipment nameplates visible**: Camera should show machinery brand and model nameplates at some point. If they don't, ask.
- **Owner present on camera**: A factory that sends only sales staff for the virtual tour (no owner or floor manager) is hiding something.

A virtual tour is 60-70% as informative as an in-person tour. It's acceptable for an initial filter; less so for a USD 50K+ first order.

## After the Tour: The 14-Day Decision Window

After visiting, give yourself 14 days to make a decision. During that window:

- **Day 1-3**: Send a thank-you note. Reference 1-2 specific observations from the tour to confirm you actually paid attention.
- **Day 4-7**: Request 3-5 yarn samples and 2-3 garment samples for lab testing. Independent lab test (SGS, Bureau Veritas, or local university textile lab) costs USD 200-500 and validates the factory's claims.
- **Day 8-10**: Reference call — ask the factory for 2-3 client references (or call known brands you've seen in their sample cards). Email the references directly.
- **Day 11-14**: Decision. Either proceed to a USD 5K-10K trial order with a 70/30 payment split (70% after delivery confirmation), or move to the next factory on your list.

If you've done this diligence, the trial order is low-risk. If the factory passes the trial, you have a supplier for the next 5+ years. If not, you've lost USD 5K-10K and learned what doesn't work — still cheaper than placing a USD 50K order with the wrong factory.

If you'd like to visit our Ordos facility, request a tour at erdosdx.com/contact — we host 30+ buyer visits per year and follow the tour structure above. For buyers who can't travel, we offer live video tours covering the same six hours of content, condensed to 45 minutes.

### Cashmere Letter of Credit Payment: A B2B Buyer's Complete 2026 Guide

*Published 2026-09-23*

How an L/C at sight protects your first cashmere order — clauses to require, fees to budget, and how an Ordos factory documents a USD 50K+ shipment for bank negotiation.

# Cashmere Letter of Credit Payment: A B2B Buyer's Complete 2026 Guide

If you're placing your first USD 30,000+ cashmere order with a Chinese factory, the payment conversation almost always lands on an **irrevocable Letter of Credit at sight (L/C)**. It protects both sides: the factory gets a bank-guaranteed payment once shipment documents match the L/C terms, and you keep payment leverage until the goods actually leave the port. But L/Cs are also where first-time importers lose money — a mismatched document set, a missing inspection certificate, or a clause the factory can't meet will stop the bank from paying and stall your cargo.

This guide explains how L/Cs work for cashmere specifically, what documents our Ordos facility routinely issues, which clauses B2B buyers should require, and what an L/C typically costs you in fees. We've processed USD 11M+ in L/C transactions over the last three years across 38 countries, so the examples below are real cases, not theory.

## What an L/C Actually Does

A Letter of Credit is a bank instrument: your issuing bank (e.g., HSBC, Deutsche Bank, Bank of America) promises to pay the beneficiary (us, the factory) once we present a set of documents that exactly match the terms you specified. The bank doesn't inspect the goods — it inspects the documents. If our commercial invoice says 1,200 kg of 2/26 Nm cashmere yarn and the packing list says 1,200 kg, the bank pays. If one document says 1,200 kg and another says 1,250 kg, the bank refuses and you have a problem.

There are three flavors B2B cashmere buyers typically use:

- **Irrevocable L/C at sight** — bank pays within 7 days of receiving conforming documents. Most common for new B2B relationships.
- **L/C with deferred payment (usance)** — bank pays 30/60/90 days after sight. Useful if you want to receive goods and sell them before paying. Slightly higher fee.
- **Confirmed L/C** — a second bank in the seller's country (often HSBC China or Bank of China) adds its guarantee on top of your issuing bank. Required if your issuing bank is unknown to the Chinese factory. Adds 1-2% fee.

For first-time orders of USD 30K-150K, the **irrevocable L/C at sight** is the standard default at our factory. Established buyers (3+ orders, USD 100K+ annual spend) can move to T/T 30/70 or OA 30 days after we have payment history.

## Required Documents for a Cashmere L/C

Our Ordos factory issues the following documents for every L/C shipment. Your L/C terms should explicitly require each one:

1. **Signed Commercial Invoice** — 3 originals + 3 copies. States product description (e.g., "100% cashmere yarn, 2/26 Nm, lot number, net weight"), unit price, total value, Incoterm, payment terms.
2. **Full set (3/3) of clean-on-board Bills of Lading** — made out "to order of [your issuing bank]", marked "freight prepaid" (for CIF) or "freight collect" (for FOB).
3. **Packing List** — net/gross weight per carton, dimensions, carton count, HS code (5108.20 for yarn, 6110.20 for knitwear, 6202 for coats).
4. **Certificate of Origin** — issued by China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT). Free for our shipments, processed in 1-2 working days.
5. **Quality Certificate / Inspection Report** — internal QC report for raw material and finished goods. For buyers requiring pre-shipment inspection (PSI), we add the SGS/Bureau Veritas/Intertek certificate here.
6. **Insurance Certificate** (for CIF/CIP shipments) — covers 110% of CIF value, ICC A clauses.
7. **Beneficiary's Certificate** — one-page letter confirming shipment was made per L/C terms. Standard clause.

Documents 1-4 are non-negotiable; documents 5-7 depend on your L/C wording and the Incoterm you've chosen. Mismatches on document 1, 3, or 4 cause 80% of L/C discrepancies — that's where B2B buyers should focus their review.

## Five Clauses That Protect B2B Buyers

A well-drafted L/C for cashmere should include these clauses:

**1. Partial shipments allowed.** Cashmere yarn is heavy (1,200 kg in our example) and may ship in two containers if the production line finishes the dye lots in stages. Forbidding partial shipments forces the factory to hold the entire order until the last lot is ready, which can add 2-4 weeks to lead time.

**2. Transshipment allowed.** Yarn and knitwear often route through Singapore or Busan before reaching the US/EU. If your L/C forbids transshipment, the goods can't load on a vessel that calls at an intermediate port — limiting shipping options and raising freight cost 15-25%.

**3. 21-day presentation period after B/L date.** Banks give sellers 21 days from the Bill of Lading date to present documents. A 14-day period is too tight — if customs clearance in Tianjin takes a week, we can't meet the document deadline. The UCP 600 default is 21 days; keep it that way.

**4. Tolerance of ±5% on quantity and value.** Yarn weight can shift slightly during dehairing (fiber loss) and knitting (yarn recovery). A 0% tolerance forces the factory to re-weigh and re-issue documents if the actual shipment is 1,195 kg instead of 1,200 kg. The standard ±5% tolerance per UCP 600 avoids this entire class of discrepancy.

**5. HS code 5108.20 (yarn) / 6110.20 (knitwear) / 6202 (coats).** Match your commercial invoice exactly to the L/C wording. If the L/C says 5108 but the invoice says 5108.20, that's a discrepancy. Be specific in your L/C draft.

These five clauses appear in roughly 90% of the L/Cs we receive from European and American buyers. If yours doesn't have them, your issuing bank can still process the L/C — but you're creating friction that may delay payment by 7-14 days if a discrepancy arises.

## Fees B2B Buyers Should Budget

L/C fees stack up on both sides. For a USD 50,000 L/C, here's the rough breakdown:

- **Issuing bank fee (buyer side)**: 0.125-0.25% of L/C value, typically USD 100-150 minimum. Some banks charge a flat USD 200-300 for small L/Cs.
- **Advising bank fee (factory side)**: USD 50-150 flat in China. The factory typically absorbs this.
- **Confirmation fee** (if confirmed L/C): 1-2% of L/C value, USD 500-1,000 on a USD 50K L/C. Only needed if your issuing bank is unknown to Chinese banks.
- **Document handling fee**: USD 50-200 per set of documents presented.
- **Discrepancy fee**: USD 50-100 per discrepancy. If documents don't match L/C terms exactly.

For a clean USD 50K L/C at sight without confirmation, total buyer-side fees are typically **USD 200-500**. That's roughly 0.5-1% of order value — much cheaper than a wire transfer fraud or a customs dispute, but real money you should budget.

## Common L/C Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

Three mistakes account for most L/C discrepancies in our experience:

**Mismatch between L/C and PO.** The purchase order says "cashmere sweater 14.5μm 2/26 Nm" but the L/C says "cashmere pullover 14-16μm 2/28 Nm". The micron range and yarn count differ. Bank refuses documents. Fix: copy the L/C wording verbatim from your PO before sending to the issuing bank. Have the factory review the L/C draft before issuance — we offer this as a free service for new buyers.

**Late shipment date.** L/Cs have a latest shipment date (typically 30-45 days after issuance). If production is delayed by even a day, the L/C expires. Fix: build a 10-day buffer into your shipment date, or include a 15-day grace period clause.

**Missing inspection certificate.** Some L/Cs require SGS or Bureau Veritas pre-shipment inspection (PSI), but the factory doesn't realize this and ships before booking the inspection. Fix: explicitly confirm with the factory that PSI is required, and book the inspection 5-7 days before shipment.

If a discrepancy does occur, you have three options: (1) ask the factory to fix and re-present documents (delays payment 7-14 days), (2) accept the discrepancy and pay (you'll be charged the discrepancy fee), or (3) negotiate with the factory for a discount to cover the discrepancy fee.

## When L/C Isn't the Right Choice

L/Cs are great for risk management on first orders and large contracts, but they have costs that don't fit every transaction:

- **Small trial orders (under USD 10,000)**: L/C fees eat 5-10% of order value. Use T/T 30/70 or PayPal for trial orders.
- **Repeat orders with established factories**: T/T 30/70 is faster (1 day to clear vs 7-14 for L/C) and cheaper.
- **Buyers with weak banking relationships**: If your issuing bank is small or unfamiliar with Asian trade, you'll be quoted high fees or refused L/C issuance. Work with HSBC, Citi, JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, or Standard Chartered for best terms.

For our existing buyers, the typical payment ladder is: T/T 30/70 for the first USD 30K trial order → L/C at sight for USD 30K-150K production orders → OA 30 days once you hit USD 100K+ annual spend. That's the path most of our 500+ active B2B clients have followed.

If you're ready to set up an L/C for your first cashmere order, request a quote at erdosdx.com/contact and we'll send you our standard L/C draft template — formatted for UCP 600 compliance with the five protective clauses above already drafted.

### Cashmere Trade Shows 2026: The Complete Calendar for B2B Cashmere Buyers

*Published 2026-09-23*

2026 cashmere trade show calendar with dates, locations, registration tips, and what to expect: SpinExpo, Première Vision, Magic, Milano Unica, and Inner Mongolia–specific expos. Plan your sourcing trips around the actual buying cycle.

# Cashmere Trade Shows 2026: The Complete Calendar for B2B Cashmere Buyers

If you source cashmere for a brand, fashion house, or retail chain, the trade show calendar shapes your buying cycle more than any other industry event. The right show connects you with mills, spinners, and garment makers who can deliver your AW26/SS27 collections on time. The wrong show burns three days and a USD 4,000 flight for nothing. This calendar covers the shows that actually matter for cashmere buyers in 2026, what each one is best for, and how to plan your visit.

We've attended 12+ cashmere-focused trade shows over the last decade, hosted booths at three of them, and walked the rest as visitors. The calendar below is the practical version — not a comprehensive industry directory, but the shows where you can see real cashmere products and talk to factory owners who can ship your order.

## The 2026 Cashmere Trade Show Calendar

Shows are organized chronologically. Most happen twice a year (February for SS collections, September-October for AW collections). Some smaller shows are annual.

### SpinExpo (Shanghai, NYC, Biella)

**Dates 2026**: SpinExpo Shanghai — March 4-6, 2026 (SS27 yarn preview). SpinExpo Shanghai — September 2-4, 2026 (AW27 yarn preview). SpinExpo New York — December 8-10, 2026 (specialty yarn showcase).

**Focus**: Yarn and fiber. SpinExpo is the most cashmere-focused yarn trade show globally. Most Chinese, Mongolian, Italian, and Scottish spinners attend. You'll see 2/26 Nm, 2/48 Nm, 100% cashmere, cashmere/silk blends, and cashmere/yak — across hundreds of mills.

**Why it matters for cashmere buyers**: If you buy yarn (rather than finished garments), SpinExpo Shanghai is essential. Two of our three yarn suppliers exhibit here annually — seeing their new collections in person lets you pre-select colors and feel yarn quality before committing to a yarn sample order. The March show is the right place to source SS27; the September show sets up AW27.

**Registration**: Free for trade buyers with business credentials (company name, tax ID, import license). Register 6-8 weeks ahead via spin-expo.com. Pre-registration gets you a buyer badge that waives the on-site registration fee (USD 50-100 otherwise).

### Première Vision (Paris, NYC)

**Dates 2026**: Première Vision Paris — February 10-12, 2026 (SS27). Première Vision Paris — September 15-17, 2026 (AW27). Première Vision New York — January 13-14, 2026 and July 14-15, 2026.

**Focus**: Premium fabric, yarn, and accessories across all fibers (wool, silk, cotton, synthetics, plus dedicated cashmere halls). Higher-end fashion houses, design studios, and brand sourcing teams attend.

**Why it matters for cashmere buyers**: PV Paris in September is where European luxury brands place AW orders for the following year. If you're a brand targeting premium retail (USD 200+ retail price points), PV is the place to be seen and to find European and Italian mills that supply into Chanel, Loro Piana, and Brunello Cucinelli. Italian mills showing here typically source their cashmere fiber from China or Mongolia — so the yarn quality is comparable to ours, but the finishing and brand reputation command a 30-50% premium.

**Registration**: Free for trade buyers, but PV uses a tiered invitation system. New buyers register via premierevision.com and request an invitation 4-6 weeks ahead. Premium buyers (those with USD 5M+ annual fiber spend) get automatic invites.

### Milano Unica (Milan)

**Dates 2026**: Milano Unica — February 4-6, 2026 (SS27). Milano Unica — July 14-16, 2026 (AW27).

**Focus**: Italian textile excellence — wool, cashmere, silk, linen, cotton. Heavily Italian mills (Loro Piana, Zegna Baruffa, Reda, Lanificio Cerruti, plus 400+ smaller mills).

**Why it matters for cashmere buyers**: Italian mills have a cachet that Asian mills don't. If your brand positioning leans "Made in Italy" or "Italian finishing", Milano Unica lets you meet the mills directly. Italian cashmere garments typically cost 50-80% more than Chinese-manufactured cashmere at the same fiber grade — partly justified by finishing and partly by the label.

**Registration**: Trade buyer registration via milanounica.it. Free with verified business credentials.

### Magic Trade Show (Las Vegas)

**Dates 2026**: Magic Las Vegas — February 9-11, 2026 (SS). Magic Las Vegas — August 17-19, 2026 (AW). Project (premium segment) co-located.

**Focus**: Finished apparel and accessories. US-market-focused. Lots of ready-to-wear cashmere sweaters, scarves, beanies from Chinese factories with US warehouses.

**Why it matters for cashmere buyers**: If you buy finished garments (not yarn), Magic is where US-based brands source the bulk of their inventory. The August edition is critical for Q4 holiday season — placing orders here in August for October-November delivery is a tight but workable cycle for stock programs.

**Registration**: USD 100-200 trade buyer pass. Register via magicfashionevents.com.

### Pure London / Pure Origin (London)

**Dates 2026**: Pure London — February 8-10, 2026 (SS27). Pure London — July 12-14, 2026 (AW27). Pure Origin co-located.

**Focus**: UK and European brands, designer collections, premium ready-to-wear. Smaller than PV but more accessible for new buyers.

**Why it matters for cashmere buyers**: Pure is where UK boutique brands and European design studios source. Less Asian factory presence than SpinExpo, but more design-led brands. If your customer base is UK/EU mid-market (USD 80-200 retail), Pure is worth a visit.

**Registration**: Free for verified trade buyers via purelondon.com.

### Inner Mongolia Cashmere Industry Expo (Ordos)

**Dates 2026**: Inner Mongolia Cashmere Industry Expo — typically held August 18-20, 2026 in Ordos (the cashmere capital of China). Date is sometimes adjusted by the local cashmere association — verify with the Ordos government commerce bureau 6 months ahead.

**Focus**: 100% Inner Mongolian cashmere. All major Ordos mills, spinners, and garment makers exhibit. Raw fiber, dehaired cashmere, yarn, fabric, finished garments — full vertical.

**Why it matters for cashmere buyers**: This is the only major trade show where you can compare 50+ Inner Mongolian cashmere mills in person. Most mills will arrange factory tours after the show — visitors typically spend 2-3 days at the expo then 2-3 days touring Ordos facilities. If your buying volume justifies a China trip (USD 50K+ annual), this show + tours is the most efficient way to evaluate 5-10 factories in one week.

**Registration**: Free or USD 50-100 depending on the year. Register via the Ordos commerce bureau or local industry associations.

### China Import & Export Fair (Canton Fair, Guangzhou)

**Dates 2026**: Canton Fair Phase 1 (industrial, electronics, textiles) — April 15-19, 2026. Canton Fair Phase 3 (apparel, textiles, fashion) — October 31 - November 4, 2026.

**Focus**: Mass-market export manufacturing. Cashmere is a small segment but exists — mostly in Phase 3.

**Why it matters for cashmere buyers**: If you need very high-volume cashmere (10,000+ pieces per SKU per color), Canton Fair has suppliers who specialize in scale. Quality is generally mid-tier (16-17μm fiber), but pricing is competitive. The expo is massive (50,000+ booths), so plan to spend 3 days minimum.

**Registration**: Free for international trade buyers. Pre-register via cantonfair.org.cn and bring business cards, passport, and your company import license.

## How to Plan Your Trade Show Visits Around the Buying Cycle

Most brands follow one of three patterns depending on volume and brand maturity:

**High-volume / 3+ years old brands (USD 500K+ annual cashmere purchase)**: Attend 2-3 shows per year. Typically SpinExpo Shanghai (March for SS, September for AW) + Première Vision Paris (September) + Canton Fair (October). Total annual trade show budget: USD 30K-60K including flights, hotels, buyer passes, dinners.

**Mid-volume / 1-3 years old (USD 50K-500K annual)**: Attend 1-2 shows per year. SpinExpo Shanghai is the most efficient — one trip covers yarn sourcing, fabric trends, and lets you visit Ordos mills on the same trip. Budget: USD 8K-15K per trip.

**New brands / low volume (under USD 50K)**: Skip shows for the first year. Use online directories (Alibaba, Made-in-China), request samples from 5-10 factories, and visit one or two factories in person if your order volume justifies it. Trade shows for new brands typically yield conversations but no orders — better to spend it on factory visits once you have specific product specs to discuss.

## What to Bring and How to Maximize Your Time

Practical tips from a decade of trade show attendance:

**Bring**: 200+ business cards (you'll give away 50-100 per day), a notebook for swatch samples with mill codes, your laptop with your fabric/yarn specifications, and a small scale (USD 30 luggage scale) to weigh yarn cones if you're sourcing yarn. Your business registration documents in case a mill asks for them on the spot.

**Don't bring**: Excess expectations. Most trade show meetings yield samples, not orders. The relationship starts at the show and matures over 6-12 months of email communication and trial orders. Don't expect to sign a USD 100K order on the spot unless you've already done 2-3 orders with the mill.

**Plan booth visits in advance**. Use the show's mobile app (all major shows have them) to mark must-see mills. Walk the show floor once without stopping to get the lay of the land, then circle back to priority booths. Most trade show apps let you pre-book meetings with exhibitors.

**Follow up within 48 hours**. Send a short email to every mill you spoke with, summarizing your conversation and next steps. Mills receive 100+ post-show emails; the ones that get a personalized follow-up get a response.

## Costs of Attending Each Show

Typical 2026 costs per attendee, excluding airfare:

| Show                    | Registration | Hotel/Night | Days | Total on-site |
|-------------------------|--------------|-------------|------|---------------|
| SpinExpo Shanghai       | Free (USD 50 on-site) | USD 100-200 | 3 | USD 500-700 |

| Pure London             | Free         | USD 200-300 | 3 | USD 700-1,000 |
| Ordos Inner Mongolia Expo | USD 50      | USD 60-100  | 3 | USD 250-400 |
| Canton Fair             | Free         | USD 100-200 | 5 | USD 600-1,200 |

Add round-trip airfare (USD 600-1,500 from US/Europe to China/Paris/Milan) and meals (USD 50-100/day). A realistic trade show trip budget ranges USD 2,500-4,500 per person per show.

## When Not to Attend a Trade Show

Trade shows are valuable, but not for every situation:

- **You don't have a clear product spec yet**: If you can't describe what you want in 3 sentences (yarn count, micron, gauge, target price), you'll waste the visit. Get the spec clear first.
- **You're still validating the market**: Before committing USD 50K to a cashmere brand, sample 5-10 factories by email and ship 3-5 small orders. The trade show is for scaling, not validating.
- **You're visiting only one or two mills**: If you've already narrowed to 1-2 mills, skip the show and visit the mills directly. More focused time, lower cost.

### Cashmere US Warehouse & Dropship Programs: 2026 B2B Buyer's Guide

*Published 2026-09-23*

How cashmere US warehouse stock programs, FBA prep, and dropshipping work for B2B buyers — pricing tiers, MOQ realities, lead times, and how Ordos-based programs cut your shipping from 30 days to 5.

# Cashmere US Warehouse & Dropship Programs: 2026 B2B Buyer's Guide

For US-based DTC brands selling cashmere, the gap between a 30-day container ship from Inner Mongolia and a 5-day Prime delivery to a Brooklyn customer is the difference between a thriving brand and a closed Shopify store. Most new cashmere brands don't realize they have a logistics problem until they're three months in, watching customers abandon carts because the estimated delivery says "mid-November" while they're shopping in October. US warehouse stock programs and dropshipping solve this — but only if you understand how they work.

This guide explains the three main fulfillment models US cashmere brands use: US warehouse stock programs (you buy and hold inventory in the US), dropshipping (you don't hold inventory, the supplier ships direct), and FBA prep (you ship to Amazon). We'll cover pricing, MOQ realities, lead times, and how to evaluate an Ordos-based supplier's US program.

## Three Fulfillment Models for US Cashmere Brands

The right model depends on your sales volume, brand positioning, and capital availability. Most brands use a hybrid — dropship for low-volume SKUs, US warehouse for hero products.

**Model 1: US Warehouse Stock Program.** You place a bulk order (typically 200-1,000 pieces per SKU) and the factory ships to a US warehouse (NJ, CA, TX are the three main hubs). You hold inventory and ship to customers yourself (or via a 3PL). Best for: hero products with predictable volume, brands doing USD 50K+/month.

**Model 2: Dropshipping.** The factory (or a US-based distributor) holds inventory and ships directly to your customer when an order comes in. You pay per-shipment + per-piece fee. Best for: testing new SKUs, low-volume products, brands doing under USD 20K/month.

**Model 3: FBA Prep.** You buy inventory, ship to Amazon's warehouse, and let Amazon handle fulfillment. Best for: Amazon-first brands, products selling well on Amazon, brands that want Prime eligibility.

Each model has different MOQ, pricing, and cash flow implications. Let's look at each in detail.

## Model 1: US Warehouse Stock Programs

How it works: You place a production order with the factory (typically 200-1,000 pieces per SKU, MOQ 100 pieces per style/color). The factory ships the finished goods by sea freight to a US warehouse — either a 3PL you select (ShipBob, ShipMonk, Deliverr, Amazon Partnered Carrier) or a factory-managed warehouse. Inventory sits in the US, and you ship to customers from there.

**Cost structure**:
- Production cost: USD 18-35 per piece for stock cashmere sweaters (varies by yarn count, gauge, micron)
- Sea freight from China to US: USD 0.30-0.80 per piece for sweaters (15-25 day transit)
- US warehousing: USD 0.50-2.00 per piece per month (varies by 3PL)
- Pick & pack fee: USD 3-6 per order + USD 0.50-1.50 per item
- US shipping to customer: USD 5-12 (USPS First Class, UPS Ground)

**MOQ realities**: Most factories require 100-200 pieces per SKU per color for stock programs. Smaller orders (50-piece trial) are possible but the per-piece cost is 20-40% higher because the factory can't amortize setup across volume. Custom Pantone colors require 5 kg per color minimum (about 25-30 pieces per color).

**Lead times**: Production 30-45 days + sea freight 15-25 days + US warehouse receiving 5-10 days = **50-80 days from PO to US warehouse stock**. Plan your first order 4-6 months before peak season (August-November for Q4 holiday).

**Common pitfall**: Brands order 500 pieces assuming they'll sell through in 60 days, then realize cashmere has longer sell-through (60-180 days for niche colors). Storage fees accumulate. Solution: order 50% of expected sales volume for first 90 days, then top up based on actual velocity.

## Model 2: Dropshipping

How it works: A US-based distributor (or a factory with US warehouse presence) holds inventory of pre-selected cashmere styles. When your customer places an order on your Shopify/WooCommerce store, the order is automatically forwarded to the distributor, who picks, packs, and ships directly to the customer. You pay a per-order fee plus the product cost.

**Cost structure**:
- Wholesale product cost: USD 22-45 per piece (higher than direct factory orders because distributor adds 15-30% margin)
- Dropship fee: USD 5-12 per order (pick, pack, label)
- US shipping to customer: USD 5-10 (often built into the dropship fee)
- Total per-piece landed cost: typically USD 30-65

**MOQ realities**: Dropship programs usually have **no MOQ** because the distributor holds inventory and amortizes risk. You can test 10 styles x 5 colors = 50 SKUs without committing to volume. This is the right model for brand testing.

**Lead times**:
- Customer order to ship: 2-5 business days (US warehouse)
- US shipping to customer: 3-7 days (USPS, UPS Ground)
- Total customer delivery: **5-12 days from order**

**Common pitfalls**:
- Lower per-piece margin (15-30% less than direct factory + US warehouse)
- Limited customization (most dropshippers stock a fixed color/style set)
- Stock-out risk on hot SKUs (the dropshipper can run out during peak season)
- Less control over packaging (typically plain poly mailer, not your branded box)

**Brand fit**: Dropshipping makes sense for brands doing under USD 20K/month, testing new markets, or running a low-SKU catalog. Once you identify your hero products and reach USD 50K+/month, transition to direct US warehouse for better margins.

## Model 3: FBA Prep (Amazon Fulfillment)

How it works: You place a production order, the factory ships to your US warehouse or directly to Amazon's warehouse (with FBA prep applied — labeling, poly bagging, bundling). Amazon holds the inventory and ships to Prime customers.

**Cost structure**:
- Production cost: same as Model 1 (USD 18-35 per piece)
- Sea freight to US: USD 0.30-0.80 per piece
- FBA prep fee: USD 0.50-2.00 per piece (labeling, poly bag, carton prep)
- Amazon FBA fees: USD 3-8 per order (pick, pack, ship, customer service) + monthly storage USD 0.50-2.50 per cubic foot
- Amazon referral fee: 15% of sale price

**MOQ realities**: Same as Model 1 (100-200 pieces per SKU minimum). Amazon FBA also has its own inventory limits — new sellers start with 500 units total storage capacity, scaling up to 100,000+ units as they sell through.

**Lead times**: 50-80 days from PO to FBA-ready inventory (same as Model 1). Then FBA receiving takes 5-14 days for Amazon to check-in your inventory.

**Common pitfalls**:
- Amazon's strict FBA prep requirements (specific label sizes, poly bag thickness, suffocation warnings). Many new sellers fail prep on first shipment and get inventory refused.
- Long-term storage fees if inventory doesn't sell (USD 6-12 per cubic foot after 365 days).
- Limited customer relationship — Amazon owns the customer data, not you.
- Cashmere is a high-value item — Amazon return rates for clothing average 15-25%, and your FBA fees apply to returns too.

**Brand fit**: FBA works for Amazon-native brands, products selling well on Amazon, and brands that want Prime eligibility without managing their own fulfillment. Most DTC brands with their own website use Model 1 (US warehouse + 3PL) instead, keeping full ownership of customer data.

## How Our Ordos-Based US Program Works

Our facility supports all three models, with a few specific characteristics worth explaining:

**Stock program** (Model 1): You order 200+ pieces per SKU in stock designs (we have 380+ stock cashmere sweaters, scarves, and beanies in white, navy, gray, camel, black). Production 30-45 days + sea freight to a US 3PL of your choice (we can recommend ShipBob, ShipMonk, or Amazon-partnered warehouses in NJ or CA). Per-piece landed cost (factory + sea freight + import duty) is USD 24-42 for sweaters, USD 8-15 for scarves, USD 9-18 for beanies depending on yarn count and micron.

**Dropship program** (Model 2): We partner with a NJ-based 3PL that holds 2,000-3,000 pieces of our stock designs at any time. When you place a customer order, the 3PL picks, packs in your branded packaging (we ship your boxes/packaging to the 3PL upfront), and ships via USPS/UPS within 2-3 business days. Dropship fee is USD 7-9 per order + product cost.

**FBA prep program** (Model 3): We prep your inventory per Amazon's FBA requirements (FNSKU labels, poly bags with suffocation warnings, bundle packaging if needed) and ship directly to Amazon's warehouse. FBA prep fee is USD 0.80-1.50 per piece depending on complexity.

The key difference vs. most cashmere dropshippers: we're the factory, so per-piece pricing is 15-25% lower than US-based distributors who source from factories like us. Our US program launched in 2023 and currently serves 40+ DTC brands across the US, Canada, and Mexico.

## Pricing Comparison: Same Sweater, Three Models

For a 14.5μm, 2/26 Nm, women's medium cashmere sweater at retail USD 89:

| Cost component              | Direct Factory | US Warehouse | Dropship | FBA Prep |
|-----------------------------|----------------|--------------|----------|----------|
| Per-piece product cost      | USD 18-22      | USD 18-22    | USD 26-32| USD 18-22|
| Sea freight (per piece)     | USD 0.0 (in production) | USD 0.40-0.60 | USD 0.0  | USD 0.40-0.60 |
| US warehousing (per month)  | USD 0          | USD 0.80-1.20| USD 0    | USD 0.50-1.00 (FBA) |
| Pick & pack (per order)     | USD 0          | USD 4-6      | USD 7-9  | USD 4-7 (FBA) |
| US shipping to customer     | USD 0          | USD 6-9      | Included | USD 0 (Prime) |
| Import duty (MFN, 0% on knit HS 6110) | USD 0 | USD 0         | USD 0    | USD 0     |
| **Total landed per order**  | USD 18-22      | USD 30-38    | USD 33-41| USD 23-30|
| **Gross margin @ $89 retail** | **75-80%**    | **57-65%**   | **54-63%**| **66-74%** |

For higher-volume brands, direct factory + US warehouse wins on margin. For lower-volume or testing brands, dropship wins on flexibility. FBA sits in between but adds Amazon's customer acquisition value.

## When to Switch Models

Most brands follow this path:
1. **Month 1-6**: Dropship for SKU testing, brand building, capital conservation.
2. **Month 6-12**: Identify top 20% of SKUs (by sales velocity). Transition those to direct factory + US warehouse.
3. **Month 12+**: Evaluate FBA prep for top sellers if Amazon channel makes sense. Continue direct fulfillment for non-Amazon channels.

Don't start with Model 1 (US warehouse) unless you have USD 50K+ working capital and validated sales forecasts. Don't stay on Model 2 (dropship) once you're consistently selling 100+ units/month of a SKU — the margin gap is too large.

If you're evaluating US warehouse or dropship programs, request a sample order through erdosdx.com/contact — we ship 2-3 stock samples within 5 days from our NJ 3PL so you can evaluate the program before committing to volume.

# 10 Types of Cashmere Yarn We Make at Our Ordos Facility: 2026 Yarn Formulation Guide

Not all cashmere yarn is created equal — and not all cashmere yarn projects need the same yarn count, fiber blend, or MOQ. At our Ordos facility, we spin ten distinct cashmere yarn formulations across four blend categories. Each formulation has been validated through full-scale production, with stable pricing for 2026 and reliable lead times for repeat orders.

This guide walks through all 10 formulations — yarn count, fiber blend ratio, typical use case, MOQ, and FOB Tianjin wholesale pricing per kilogram — so a private-label buyer or knitwear brand can match the right yarn to their product and retail tier.

## How We Organize Our Cashmere Yarn Formulations

Our 10 yarn formulations fall into four blend categories:

| Category | Formulations | Typical MOQ | Position in Catalog |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pure Cashmere** (100% cashmere) | 4 | 50 kg per count | Standard + premium tier |
| **Cashmere + Wool** | 2 | 50 kg per count | Entry-level to mid-tier |

The pure-cashmere range covers gauge needs from chunky-weaving (1/4.3NM, 1/6.5NM) to fine-worsted (3/68NM). The blend categories address price-tier diversification: cashmere-wool blends sit at the entry-level, cashmere-specialty blends at the mid-to-premium tier, and signature blends (YARK, Taiji Stone) become brand-differentiating SKUs.

**Use case**: Standard machine-knitting and weaving yarn for sweaters, scarves, accessories

Common in mid-tier retail programs that want a "cashmere" hand-feel signal at price points below the 100% cashmere threshold.

## How to Choose the Right Formulation

Most private-label buyers fall into one of three selection patterns:

**Pattern A — Classic Cashmere Program** (the most common)
Default to **2/26NM 100% cashmere** for sweaters and scarves. Use **3/68NM** for premium-tier lightweight layering. Add **2/36NM** if you need a mid-weight jersey.

**Pattern B — Price-Tier Diversification** (retail brands with multiple price points)
Stock 100% cashmere (premium tier), cashmere-wool 30/70 (mid tier), and cashmere-linen 65/35 (transitional tier) across 3 SKUs.

**Pattern C — Signature Product Line** (boutique brands seeking differentiation)
Build your brand around one of the signature blends — YARK 50/50 or Taiji Stone 10/40/50. These yarns become brand-defining SKUs that competitors cannot easily replicate.

### What is the minimum order for cashmere yarn?

50 kg per count for standard formulations (pure cashmere, cashmere-wool, cashmere-specialty). 100 kg per count for signature blends (YARK, Taiji Stone).

### What is the lead time for cashmere yarn orders?

Stock counts in stock colors: 7–10 days for 50–200 kg orders. Custom Pantone: 25–35 days bulk production after lab dip approval. Signature blends add 10–15 days for raw material sourcing.

### Can you blend custom ratios beyond the 10 stock formulations?

Yes — for orders 200 kg+, we can spin custom ratios between 2/16 and 2/80 Nm. Common custom ratios include 50/50 cashmere-wool for mid-tier positioning and 80/20 cashmere-silk for ultra-premium lines. Custom blends add 4–6 weeks to lead time.

### What micron grade is your cashmere?

14.5–15.5 μm premium (Alashan / Ordos Albas white), 15.5–16.5 μm mid-grade. Each yarn batch ships with lot micron documentation and fiber origin certificate.

### How is cashmere yarn packaged for export?

Standard: 500 g or 1 kg cones in polybag, 20–25 kg per carton. Custom packaging (hanks, larger cones, branded labels) available from 100 kg orders.

### Can you do a sample before placing the bulk order?

Yes. Sample lead time is 7–10 days for 1–5 kg samples. Sample cost USD 8–25 per kg depending on the formulation, refundable against bulk order of 100 kg+.

# 2026 Autumn Cashmere Sweater OEM Order Cutoff: Last Booking Dates for Q4 & Holiday Delivery

# 2026 Autumn Cashmere Sweater OEM Order Cutoff: Last Booking Dates for Q4 & Holiday Delivery

Every September, the same email lands in our inbox from buyers across the EU, US, and Japan: *"We need 800 cashmere sweaters in our warehouse by November 20th for Black Friday and holiday pre-orders. Can you still take the order?"* The honest answer is sometimes yes, sometimes no — and the difference comes down to a single number: how many weeks of production are actually left between today and your required delivery date.

This guide publishes the **final order cutoff dates for autumn 2026 production** at our Ordos factory, broken down by product type, MOQ, and decoration complexity. If you are sourcing private-label cashmere sweaters, cardigans, or knit accessories for Q4 2026 / Holiday 2026 / early Q1 2027 delivery, the dates below tell you whether your order is still feasible — and what trade-offs you will face if you book late.

## Why Cutoff Dates Exist in Cashmere OEM

Unlike polyester or cotton knitwear, cashmere production is constrained by a hard biological clock. The dehairing season in Inner Mongolia runs from April to June; by September, the raw material for the year is already allocated to yarn spinners and we are deep into the dyeing-spinning-knitting pipeline. Once our knitting lines, dyeing vats, and finishing capacity are booked, adding more orders means displacing existing customers — which is something we will not do.

This is why every autumn we publish cutoff dates publicly. Buyers who book before the cutoff get:

- **Confirmed production slot** on the knitting line.
- **Yarn allocation** from our 2026 dehairing pool.
- **Realistic shipping windows** to EU/US/JP ports.
- **No expedite surcharge** (late orders after the cutoff face 15-25% expedite fees, if capacity exists at all).

Buyers who book after the cutoff either pay a premium for line re-scheduling, simplify the garment to fit a shorter window, or wait for Q1 2027 production.

## What Happens If You Miss the Cutoff

Three options, in order of cost:

### Option 1: Expedite with Surcharge (Capacity Available)

If we have a partial gap on the knitting line — for example, a buyer cancelled or downsized — we can slot in late orders with a **15-25% expedite surcharge**. This surcharge covers overtime labor, shifted yarn allocation, and the risk premium. Typical expedite windows:

- 1-2 weeks past cutoff: 15% surcharge, ex-works delayed by 7-10 days.
- 3-4 weeks past cutoff: 20-25% surcharge, ex-works delayed by 14-21 days.

Availability is by inquiry only. Do not assume capacity exists.

### Option 2: Simplify the Garment

Strip out the bottleneck step. Common simplifications:

- **Custom yarn → stock yarn**: saves 2-3 weeks. You accept our standard color card (currently 42 stock colors).
- **Complex stitch → plain knit**: saves 1-2 weeks. Loses design differentiation but gains speed.
- **Embroidery/print after knitting instead of in-knit**: saves 1 week. Acceptable for chest logos, not allover patterns.
- **Custom labels → stock labels with sticker overlay**: saves 3-5 days. Common for sub-300 pc trial orders.

### Option 3: Move to Q1 2027 Production

If the order cannot realistically hit Q4 2026, we will quote for **Q1 2027 production** (ex-works January-February 2027). This is the default for new design development and orders that need full custom yarn + complex stitch + custom trims. Q1 2027 slots open for booking on **2026-10-15**.

### Cashmere Hoodie Wholesale Guide: Knit Gauge, Yarn Count & Construction Specs for B2B Buyers

*Published 2026-09-16*

Cashmere hoodies sit at the intersection of knitwear and athleisure, with wholesale FOB Tianjin pricing of $32–48 per piece and retail markups of 5–8x. This guide breaks down the gauge, yarn count, weight, and construction decisions that determine whether your private-label hoodie program succeeds.

# Cashmere Hoodie Wholesale Guide: Knit Gauge, Yarn Count & Construction Specs for B2B Buyers

Cashmere hoodies occupy a specific corner of the cashmere market — too casual for a traditional V-neck cardigan buyer, too refined for an athleisure program. The B2B buyers who do well with cashmere hoodies are usually building one of three product lines: premium athleisure (¥800–2,500 retail), boutique layering pieces ($180–450 retail), or corporate-casual uniform programs (where the hood replaces a formal collar). Each program has different specs, different MOQ requirements, and different risk profiles.

This guide walks through the engineering and sourcing decisions that determine whether a cashmere hoodie program succeeds at your retail tier. It is written from the perspective of an Ordos facility that produces both jacquard cable-knit hoodies and simpler flat-knit hoodies for private-label buyers.

## Cashmere Hoodie vs Cashmere Crewneck Pullover: When to Add the Hood

A hoodie adds roughly $4–8 to the wholesale unit cost versus a comparable crewneck pullover. The hood (with or without drawcord) requires:

- **An additional knitted piece** (the hood itself) — typically 60–90g for a cashmere hood
- **A drawcord channel** — usually a contrasting cashmere cord with metal or fabric tips
- **Front pocket integration** if specified (kangaroo or side-seam welt pockets add $1.50–3.00)
- **Button-front or zip-front closure** as an alternative to the pullover — adds $2.50–5.50

If your retail program is already selling cashmere crewnecks at $180+ retail, the marginal cost of adding a hooded version is small relative to the consumer-perceived novelty. If you are below $120 retail, the hood cost premium is harder to absorb.

## Construction: Pullover vs Zip-Front vs Button-Front

Three hoodie constructions are common in cashmere:

**Pullover hoodie** (no front closure): the simplest and most common. Wholesale $32–42 per piece, MOQ 100. Best for boutique layering programs.

**Button-front hoodie** (full button placket, 5–7 buttons): more structured look, blends hoodie aesthetics with cardigan styling. Wholesale $36–48 per piece, MOQ 100. Best for transitional-season retail and corporate-casual uniform programs.

**Zip-front hoodie**: requires metal or plastic zipper integration, more complex construction. Wholesale $38–52 per piece, MOQ 200. Best for premium athleisure where the zip is a brand feature.

## Knit Gauge and Yarn Count

**Gauge 5gg – 7gg (chunky)**: 380–480g hoodie weight. Visible cable-knit or jacquard texture, drapes heavily, premium gift-set aesthetic. The most common gauge for cable-knit cashmere hoodies.

**Gauge 9gg – 12gg (mid)**: 280–360g hoodie weight. Smooth or lightly patterned surface, balanced structure. Standard for commercial cashmere hoodie production.

**Gauge 14gg (fine)**: 220–280g hoodie weight. Smooth surface, refined drape, dressier aesthetic. Common for athleisure-tier cashmere hoodies sold at premium retail.

**Yarn count**: 2/26 Nm woolen-spun for chunky knits (most common); 2/48 Nm worsted-spun for fine-gauge pieces (premium tier). Worsted-spun yarn adds 30–40% to the yarn cost.

## Fiber and Origin

All cashmere hoodie programs at our Ordos facility use Grade A Mongolian cashmere at 14.5–15.5μm. Cashmere finer than 14.5μm (Grade A+) is available for premium athleisure programs at +25% fiber cost.

**Sustainability**: Sustainable Fibre Alliance (SFA) chain-of-custody certification is available for buyers requiring herder-welfare documentation. OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification is included by default for all garments.

## Standard Specification: Cable-Knit Cashmere Hoodie

The most-requested cashmere hoodie spec at our facility is a jacquard cable-knit pullover with drawcord hood, kangaroo pocket, and ribbed cuffs and hem. Standard specs:

| Specification | Standard Cable-Knit Hoodie |
|---|---|

- **Drawcord color and tip material** — brushed metal, fabric-wrapped, leather (premium), MOQ 100 pieces
- **Kangaroo pocket or side-seam welt pockets** — design choice
- **Custom button material** for button-front versions — horn, corozo, mother-of-pearl (premium), plastic (economy)
- **Branded care label** and hangtag, MOQ 100 pieces
- **Custom packaging** — branded polybag, tissue, rigid box, MOQ 100 pieces

## Common Mistakes B2B Buyers Make

**Mistake 1: Specifying a fine-gauge 14gg hoodie for a gift-set program.** The yarn becomes too thin to express cable-knit or jacquard patterns. Use 5gg – 9gg for pattern programs; reserve 14gg for plain-knit athleisure.

**Mistake 2: Forgetting to specify hood lining.** A single-layer cashmere hood against bare skin can feel scratchy on sensitive users. A double-layer hood or jersey lining adds $1.50–2.50 per piece and dramatically improves wearer comfort.

**Mistake 3: Underestimating the drawcord cost.** Premium metal or leather-tipped drawcords add $1.20–2.80 per piece. For 1,000-piece orders this becomes a meaningful line item.

**Mistake 4: Skipping sample fitting on size S and XXL.** Cashmere hoodie sizing is more forgiving than woven garments, but the hood-to-shoulder drop still varies. Always request size-run samples before bulk production.

## Sustainability and Origin

All cashmere for our hoodie program is sourced from the Alashan and Ordos goat herds, dehairing April–June each year. SFA certification is available for buyers who require herder-welfare documentation.

For brands with regenerative-wool positioning, a 70% cashmere / 30% merino blend is available at -8% fiber cost. The blend improves durability for athleisure-tier wear.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the typical MOQ for a cashmere hoodie?

MOQ is 100 pieces per design in stock colors. Custom Pantone from 5 kg per color (about 100 hoodies). Custom drawcord colors and tip materials from 100 pieces.

### Can I get a sample hoodie before placing the bulk order?

Yes. Sample lead time is 7–10 days. Sample cost USD 35–80 per piece, refundable against the first bulk order over 300 pieces. Size-run samples (S / M / L) recommended.

### What gauge is best for a cable-knit cashmere hoodie?

5gg – 7gg chunky knit. The yarn weight expresses the cable pattern definition. 9gg is acceptable for fine cables; 14gg is too smooth for textured patterns.

### Can I add a zip-front version to the same program?

Yes. Zip-front cashmere hoodies use the same yarn and gauge specs but require a different pattern piece set. MOQ 200 pieces for zip-front versions.

### What is the lead time for a 500-piece custom Pantone order?

Approximately 50–65 days total: 7–10 days lab dip, 35–40 days bulk production, 3–5 days QC, plus 20–35 days sea freight.

### Cashmere Knit Beanie vs Wool Beanie: B2B Buying Guide for Wholesale Buyers (FW 2026)

*Published 2026-09-16*

Cashmere knit beanies retail for $90–180 and wholesale at $9–16 per piece, while wool beanies retail for $25–55 and wholesale at $3–7. This guide breaks down fiber cost, knit construction, gauge, and origin specs so a private-label buyer can choose correctly.

# Cashmere Knit Beanie vs Wool Beanie: B2B Buying Guide for Wholesale Buyers (FW 2026)

Every autumn, the same question arrives from private-label buyers and boutique owners across the EU, US, and Japan: *"Should we run a cashmere beanie program this year, or is wool close enough?"* The honest answer depends on what you are building — a premium gift, an everyday winter staple, or a corporate uniform — and the decision is rarely about fiber alone. It is about fiber **plus** gauge **plus** finishing **plus** minimum order quantity.

This guide walks through the engineering specs, pricing tiers, and sourcing realities that determine whether a cashmere knit beanie program makes sense for your brand. It is written from the perspective of an Ordos factory that produces both cashmere and merino wool beanies for 23+ years.

## Cashmere Beanie vs Wool Beanie: Side-by-Side Specs

| Specification | Cashmere Beanie | Merino Wool Beanie |
|---|---|---|
| Fiber | Grade A Mongolian 14.5–15.5μm | 18.5–21.5μm merino |
| Yarn count | 2/26 Nm woolen-spun | 2/28 Nm woolen-spun |
| Gauge | 7gg – 12gg | 7gg – 14gg |
| Weight per beanie | 38–55g | 45–65g |
| Hand-feel | Soft, low-pilling, drapes | Springy, slightly textured |
| Thermal rating (ISO 1107) | High — fibers trap more air per gram | Medium-High |
| Wholesale FOB Tianjin | USD 9.20–16.50 / piece | USD 3.50–6.80 / piece |
| Retail markup (typical) | 6–10x | 3–5x |
| Retail price range | USD 90–180 | USD 25–55 |
| Lead time | 25–35 days + QC + freight | 20–30 days + QC + freight |
| MOQ (per design/color) | 100 pcs | 200 pcs |
| Sample cost | USD 25–60 / piece, refundable | USD 8–20 / piece, refundable |

The single biggest practical difference is **hand-feel against the forehead**. Cashmere at 14.5μm has a fiber diameter roughly 30% thinner than fine merino. For buyers building premium gift sets or resort wear, this gap is the entire value proposition. For buyers building outdoor or uniform programs, the gap matters less and wool's durability may actually be preferable.

## When to Choose Cashmere

Cashmere knit beanies make sense for these B2B programs:

- **Premium gift sets** bundled with scarves, gloves, or shawls for luxury retail
- **Resort and travel wear** for high-end hotel chains, first-class airline partnerships
- **Boutique private-label collections** sold at $120–250 retail
- **Corporate executive gifting** for end-of-year client presents
- **Cashmere-only collections** where a wool piece would break the brand promise

If your retail price floor is below USD 60, cashmere is the wrong fiber. The economics break — your margin absorbs the cost differential before the customer experiences the hand-feel benefit.

## When to Choose Wool

Merino wool beanies work better for these B2B programs:

- **Outdoor and ski-resort uniform programs** where durability matters more than softness
- **School and team uniforms** at high volume (3,000+ pieces)
- **Eco-positioned brands** where the regenerative-wool story is part of the product
- **Mid-market retail** at USD 30–60 price points
- **Cold-weather workwear** for industrial and outdoor use

Wool is also the better choice when the program requires aggressive washing — merino tolerates machine washing on wool cycle far better than cashmere.

## Knit Construction: Gauge, Yarn Count, and Fit

Three numbers determine the final beanie: **gauge** (needles per inch), **yarn count** (Nm), and **crown height**.

**Gauge 7gg – 9gg (chunky knit)**: 38–55g beanie weight, visible rib texture, drapes softly. Best for cashmere and gift sets. Requires more yarn per piece, which raises fiber cost.

**Gauge 10gg – 12gg (mid-gauge)**: 32–45g beanie weight, balanced hand-feel, more shape-retention. The standard for both cashmere and wool commercial production.

**Gauge 14gg (fine-gauge)**: 24–35g beanie weight, smooth surface, dressier look. Most common for wool beanies sold at lower retail tiers. Rare for cashmere because the yarn becomes too thin to fully express the fiber benefit.

**Yarn count 2/26 Nm**: the industry standard for both fibers. Worsted-spun 2/48 Nm gives a smoother, more refined cashmere beanie for premium gift sets — but adds 30–40% to yarn cost.

**Crown height 18–22 cm**: standard. A 24cm "slouchy" beanie uses 12–18% more yarn and is a deliberate design choice for the youth market.

## Cuff, Fold, and Pom Options

Most cashmere beanies use a **folded cuff** (5–7cm turn-up at the bottom), which adds 8–12g of yarn but gives the wearer two wearing styles and signals premium quality. A **rib-knit cuff** (3–4cm, no fold) is more common on wool beanies for uniform programs.

Fur pom-poms are not used on cashmere beanies from our facility — the fiber and price point don't match the aesthetic. A **yarn pom** (matching cashmere or merino) is available from MOQ 200 pieces and adds $1.20–1.80 to the unit cost.

## MOQ, Lead Time, and Production Calendar

For FW 2026 / Q4 2026 / Holiday 2026 delivery at our Ordos facility:

| Order size | Cashmere beanie lead time | Wool beanie lead time |
|---|---|---|
| 100–500 pcs | 25–30 days | 20–25 days |
| 500–2,000 pcs | 30–35 days | 25–30 days |
| 2,000+ pcs | 35–45 days | 30–40 days |
| Custom Pantone (5+ kg per color) | +7–10 days lab dip | +5–7 days lab dip |
| Branded care label | +3 days | +3 days |
| Custom packaging | +5–7 days | +5–7 days |

**Sample timeline**: 7–10 days for cashmere samples, 5–7 days for wool. Sample cost refundable against first bulk order over 300 pieces.

## Customization Options for Private Label

From our Ordos facility:

- **Woven label**: sewn into the back seam, 2×1cm to 4×2cm, MOQ 100 pieces
- **Embroidered logo**: on the folded cuff, MOQ 200 pieces
- **Custom Pantone color**: from 5 kg per color (about 100 beanies), 7-day lab dip
- **Custom packaging**: branded boxes, dust bags, or polybags, MOQ 100 pieces
- **Care card insert**: branded care instruction card, MOQ 500 pieces

All customization is documented per shipment with lot references and finishing records.

## Common Mistakes B2B Buyers Make

**Mistake 1: Specifying a 14gg cashmere beanie for a gift set.** The yarn is too thin to express cashmere's hand-feel benefit. Use 7gg – 10gg for gift-set programs.

**Mistake 2: Underestimating yarn consumption for cuffed beanies.** A cuffed cashmere beanie uses 18–25% more yarn than a rib-cuff version. Budget and MOQ calculations should account for this.

**Mistake 3: Ordering wool beanies for tropical markets.** A 60g wool beanie is uncomfortable above 25°C. For tropical retail or resort wear, specify 35g or lighter.

**Mistake 4: Skipping the OEKO-TEX certification request.** Premium retail increasingly requires OEKO-TEX Standard 100. Our facility holds certification and can include the certificate per shipment.

## Sustainability and Origin

All cashmere for our beanie program is sourced from the Alashan and Ordos goat herds, dehairing April–June each year. The Sustainable Fibre Alliance (SFA) certification is available for buyers who require herder-welfare documentation, adding 3–5 days to the order process.

For wool beanie programs, regenerative merino from Inner Mongolia cooperative farms is available from MOQ 500 pieces, with full chain-of-custody documentation.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the typical MOQ for a cashmere knit beanie?

MOQ is 100 pieces per design in stock colors. Custom Pantone from 5 kg per color (about 100 beanies). Branded labels and packaging from 100 pieces.

### Can I get a sample beanie before placing the bulk order?

Yes. Sample lead time is 7–10 days for cashmere, 5–7 days for wool. Sample cost USD 25–60 per piece (cashmere) or USD 8–20 per piece (wool), refundable against the first bulk order over 300 pieces.

### What gauge is best for a premium gift-set cashmere beanie?

7gg – 9gg chunky knit. The visible rib texture and yarn weight express the cashmere hand-feel benefit. 14gg is too refined for gift-set programs.

### Can I get the same beanie in both cashmere and wool?

Yes. We can run matched designs across both fibers from the same Pantone reference. Cashmere at 100 pieces MOQ, wool at 200 pieces MOQ per design.

### What is the lead time for a 1,000-piece custom Pantone order?

Approximately 40–50 days total: 7–10 days lab dip, 30–35 days bulk production, 3–5 days QC, plus 20–35 days sea freight (depending on destination). Air freight reduces transit to 5–7 days if faster delivery is required.

### Cashmere Mock Neck Sweater Wholesale: B2B Spec, Sizing & MOQ Guide

*Published 2026-09-16*

Cashmere mock neck sweaters wholesale at $32–48 per piece, retail at $180–340. This guide covers mock depth, gauge, sizing, and MOQ for B2B buyers building private-label half-turtleneck programs.

# Cashmere Mock Neck Sweater Wholesale: B2B Spec, Sizing & MOQ Guide

The cashmere mock neck sits in the small but growing segment between crew neck and full turtleneck. It covers the throat without bunching, layers cleanly under a jacket without bulk, and reads as more polished than a crew without committing to the formality of a full turtleneck. For B2B buyers building FW collections at the $180–340 retail tier, the mock neck has become a quiet best-seller — not as universal as the crew, but with higher average order value.

This guide walks through the mock depth, gauge, sizing, and finishing decisions that determine whether a cashmere mock neck program succeeds.

## Cashmere Mock Neck vs Crew Neck vs Turtleneck

| Construction | Mock Neck | Crew Neck | Full Turtleneck |
|---|---|---|---|
| Collar height | 3–5cm fold | None (rib trim only) | 14–20cm fold |
| Throat coverage | Partial | None | Full |
| Layering under jacket | Excellent | Excellent | Poor (bunches) |
| Formality | Smart-casual | Casual | Casual-to-business |
| Best retail tier | $180–340 | $140–280 | $180–360 |
| Wholesale FOB Tianjin | $32–48 / piece | $28–42 / piece | $34–50 / piece |
| MOQ | 100 pcs | 50 pcs | 100 pcs |
| Lead time | 30–35 days | 25–30 days | 30–40 days |

The mock neck is more expensive than the crew because the collar stand requires the same careful finishing as a full turtleneck, but uses less yarn. The result is a price point very close to the full turtleneck despite using less fiber.

## Mock Depth Specification

The mock depth (collar height when worn) determines the mock's character:

**3cm shallow mock**: reads as a thicker crew neck. Refined, business-appropriate. Best for office-wear programs.

**4cm standard mock**: the most-requested depth. Versatile, layers cleanly, works under a jacket or alone. The default for FW 2026.

**5cm deep mock**: bolder, more fashion-forward. Reads as a half-turtleneck. Suits boutique and editorial retail.

**6cm+ deep mock**: rare for cashmere; reads as a shortened turtleneck. Risk of bunching under a jacket.

The mock depth specification in the bulk contract should include the **worn height** (3cm, 4cm, 5cm) and the **flat knit height** (5cm, 6cm, 7cm) — the difference accounts for the fold behavior.

## Construction Details

**Collar stand**: knit as a separate piece, joined to the body with a linking seam. The seam must be flat (no bulk against the throat) and recover fully after washing.

**Collar fold behavior**: should fold cleanly without flipping or rolling. Specify the fold line in the pattern piece (typically 2–3cm from the top edge).

**Body gauge vs collar gauge**: typically 1 gauge finer for the collar (12gg body, 14gg collar) to give the collar a tighter, more polished look. Mismatched gauge is a common source of bulk and uneven fold behavior.

**Cuff and hem**: standard 2×2 rib, 6–8cm width. Matching body gauge or one gauge finer.

## Common Mistakes B2B Buyers Make

**Mistake 1: Specifying the same gauge for body and collar.** This creates a bulky, unflattering collar. The collar should be one gauge finer for the cleanest fold.

**Mistake 2: Skipping the fold-behavior test.** The mock depth specification only matters if the fold behaves correctly. Always test a sample collar under live conditions (washed and worn for 30 minutes) before bulk production.

**Mistake 3: Forgetting to specify collar recovery target.** Cashmere collars stretch with wear. Specify 90%+ recovery after 30 minutes in the bulk contract.

**Mistake 4: Underestimating the collar yarn consumption.** The collar stand adds 15–25g of yarn per mock neck versus a crew neck. Budget this for both cost and lead-time.

**Mistake 5: Specifying a 5cm+ mock for office-wear programs.** The deep mock reads as too casual for office settings. Reserve 5cm+ for boutique and editorial retail.

# Cashmere Polo Sweater Wholesale: B2B Style Guide (Polo vs Crew vs Mock Neck Comparison)

Cashmere polo-collar sweaters have become one of the most-requested knit constructions at our Ordos facility over the past two FW seasons. The reason is structural: the polo collar (2–3 button placket, fold-over or ribbed knit collar) occupies a niche between casual and refined that the standard crew neck and the V-neck cardigan don't quite fill. For private-label buyers building collections at the $160–320 retail tier, the polo construction is increasingly a core style — not a one-off curiosity.

This guide compares polo, crew, mock neck, and V-neck constructions so B2B buyers can choose the right collar for their brand positioning.

## Cashmere Polo Sweater vs Crew Neck vs Mock Neck: Quick Comparison

## When to Choose Cashmere Polo

The polo construction works best for these B2B programs:

- **Smart-casual retail programs** targeting 30–55 year-old professional buyers
- **Resort and country-club collections** where a fold collar signals refinement
- **Corporate-casual uniform programs** where a polo replaces a formal shirt collar
- **Bridal and occasionwear programs** where the polo construction works under a jacket

Avoid the polo for:
- **Athleisure or loungewear** programs (use crew or hooded)

### Cashmere V-Neck Cardigan Wholesale: B2B Gauge & Yarn Count Buying Guide

*Published 2026-09-16*

# Cashmere V-Neck Cardigan Wholesale: B2B Gauge & Yarn Count Buying Guide

The V-neck cardigan is the most-requested cashmere knitwear construction at our Ordos facility. It is also the most-variable in spec: V-depth, placket width, button count, button material, and gauge can all shift the final product from a $140 retail casual layer to a $340 retail refined staple. For B2B buyers, getting these specs right at the sample stage is the difference between a successful program and a re-order disaster.

This guide walks through the gauge, yarn count, placket, and finishing decisions that determine whether a cashmere V-neck cardigan program succeeds at your retail tier.

The three tiers correspond to three retail audiences: refined (office-wear, smart-casual, gift sets), chunky premium (boutique casual, layering programs), and heavy gauge (high-end outerwear-replacement programs).

## Choosing the Right Gauge for Your Retail Tier

**5gg heavy gauge**: 480–620g cardigan weight. Visibly chunky knit, drapes heavily, reads as outerwear. The right choice for FW 2026 luxury programs where the cardigan replaces a jacket. Most expensive in fiber cost.

**7gg chunky**: 380–480g cardigan weight. Visible knit texture, premium casual aesthetic. The standard for boutique cashmere cardigan programs.

**12gg refined**: 280–340g cardigan weight. Smooth surface, refined drape, office-appropriate. The most-requested gauge for B2B programs — works under a jacket or alone.

**14gg fine-gauge**: 220–280g cardigan weight. Smooth drape, dressier aesthetic. Common for office-wear programs where the cardigan substitutes for a sweater vest.

For FW 2026, the 12gg refined tier is the most-requested at our facility. The 7gg chunky tier is the fastest-growing segment, driven by the layering-trend.

## V-Depth and Placket Construction

**V-depth** (the distance from the shoulder seam to the V point):
- 18cm: modest, office-appropriate, layers well over a collared shirt
- 20cm: standard, suits most retail programs
- 22cm: deeper, more fashion-forward, suits smart-casual retail
- 24cm+: very deep, statement piece, suits editorial retail

**Placket width** (the reinforced front band on each side of the V):
- 2.5cm: refined, suits 12gg cardigans
- 3cm: standard, suits 7gg chunky
- 3.5cm: chunky, suits 5gg heavy gauge

**Button count and spacing**: 5 buttons is standard for cashmere cardigans (V-depth 20–22cm). 6 buttons for deeper V (22–26cm). 4 buttons for shorter V (16–18cm). Button spacing should be 9–10cm for refined, 10–11cm for chunky.

**Rib trim**: the V-neck rib trim is the most visible detail. Specify rib width (2–2.5cm standard), rib gauge (matching body gauge), and rib fold behavior (lay-flat or fold-over).
