### Good Cashmere Standard 2026: Updated Animal Welfare and Traceability Requirements for Cashmere B2B Programs

*Published 2026-08-28*

A dated working note on the Good Cashmere Standard (GCS) updates issued by the Aid by Trade Foundation in 2026, the new animal welfare and traceability requirements that apply to certified cashmere, and the records a buyer should expect from a GCS-aligned supplier.

## What the Good Cashmere Standard is, and who maintains it

The Good Cashmere Standard (GCS) is an independent standard for cashmere fibre, set and administered by the Aid by Trade Foundation (AbTF). The standard defines animal welfare, environmental, and chain-of-custody criteria for raw cashmere, and provides a labelled pathway for downstream products. The AbTF publishes the standard documents and the list of certified farms, dehairing facilities and brands. [1](https://www.goodcashmerestandard.com/)

In 2026, the AbTF released an updated version of the Good Cashmere Standard with refined animal welfare criteria and expanded traceability requirements for the dehairing and trading stages. The updates apply to all newly certified operations from 1 January 2026; existing certified operations transition during 2026 in line with the AbTF's published timetable. [1](https://www.goodcashmerestandard.com/)

#### Where to confirm the current version

The most reliable reference for the standard's current text, the transition timetable and the list of certified operations is the AbTF's own publication. Earlier reference materials, including older blog posts or buyer guides, may not reflect the 2026 revisions. When confirming compliance or preparing an inquiry, treat the AbTF site as the canonical source rather than secondary summaries. [1](https://www.goodcashmerestandard.com/)

#### Practical areas updated for 2026

Based on the AbTF's published updates, three areas are most relevant to a cashmere B2B buyer:

1. **Animal welfare criteria** — the standard already covers grazing, shelter, handling and shearing. The 2026 update raises expectations on cold-weather shelter, the timing and method of fibre collection, and the documentation of veterinary care. The objective is to align GCS with broader animal welfare standard practice without changing the underlying principle of combing rather than shearing. [1](https://www.goodcashmerestandard.com/)

2. **Chain-of-custody documentation** — the updated standard expands the requirement to record fibre origin, herd type, and the dehairing facility for each lot traded under the standard. The records must be auditable; the AbTF publishes the audit frequency and the certification body's scope. [1](https://www.goodcashmerestandard.com/)

3. **Brand and retailer obligations** — brands and retailers using the GCS label must keep the labelled fibre traceable through processing stages. This is the practical impact on a private-label or retail program sourcing GCS-aligned cashmere. [1](https://www.goodcashmerestandard.com/)

These are administrative controls, not a guarantee of any specific outcome. The actual scope, evidence and certification body decision depend on the AbTF's published rules and the buyer's product category.

#### What a B2B buyer can confirm with a cashmere supplier

For a private-label, retail, or wholesale program using GCS-aligned cashmere, the following records are typically worth confirming in writing:

| Area | Practical record to ask for | Why it is useful now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Certification status | GCS certificate number and scope, valid until date | Confirms the operation is currently certified |
| Origin | Region, herd type, list of certified farms | Supports fibre origin claims and DPP-style records |
| Dehairing | Certified dehairing facility name and address | Demonstrates chain-of-custody compliance |
| Lot reference | Internal lot, bale or shipment reference linked to origin records | Allows traceability per shipment |
| Brand licence | Brand or retailer's own GCS label licence number, if applicable | Confirms the downstream user is licensed to use the mark |
| Documentation owner | Which party is responsible for each record | Clarifies the data request process |

The actual scope depends on the buyer's product, destination and brand policy. Treat this list as a starting point for an inquiry, not as a standard checklist.

#### How GCS relates to other cashmere frameworks

GCS is one of several frameworks a cashmere buyer may need to evaluate together. Each framework has its own scope:

- **Textile Exchange Recycled Cashmere Standard** — for cashmere fibre recovered from pre- or post-consumer textile waste.
- **OEKO-TEX Standard 100** — for finished textile products at the consumer level.
- **EU CSDDD / DPP** — chain-of-custody records for the largest companies selling textile products in the EU.

A cashmere supplier may participate in one or several frameworks. The buyer should clarify which framework applies to each material or product, rather than assume a single certification covers everything.

#### References

1. Aid by Trade Foundation, [The Good Cashmere Standard](https://www.goodcashmerestandard.com/), accessed 28 August 2026.

For practical context on the broader EU regulatory landscape affecting cashmere, see the [EU CSDDD for textile supply chains](/en/blog/eu-csddd-textile-supply-chain-2026/) and the [EU Textile Digital Product Passport update](/en/blog/eu-textile-dpp-registry-2026-update/).

### Japan and Korea Cashmere Knitwear Import Market: What B2B Buyers Should Confirm in 2026

*Published 2026-08-28*

A dated working note on the Japan and South Korea cashmere knitwear import markets, the buyer profiles, import flow considerations, and practical records a cashmere manufacturer should expect from Japanese and Korean B2B buyers in 2026.

## What we observed at a glance

Japan and South Korea are the largest Asian cashmere knitwear import markets outside Greater China. The two markets differ in buyer profile, product preference and import flow, but share several practical concerns: premium grade selection, lot consistency, documentation requirements and brand-led marketing claims. This note covers both markets for comparison; specific buyer assumptions should be confirmed per inquiry.

The numbers cited below are working estimates drawn from publicly available trade statistics and the patterns observed at our facility. Where a figure is precise, the source is named; where it is directional, it is described as such.

#### Japan — premium grade, brand-led, low MOQ per style

The Japan cashmere knitwear import market is dominated by:

- **Luxury houses** (e.g. the established Japanese luxury conglomerates and the European houses with Japanese subsidiaries) sourcing premium-grade yarn for in-house knitwear programs.
- **Mid-tier Japanese brands** that produce seasonal knitwear for the domestic department store and select-shop retail channels.
- **Boutique brands and ateliers** that work with small lots and prioritise grade, hand-feel and pattern development.

Key practical considerations for Japan-bound cashmere programs:

- **Grade preference**: Japanese buyers typically specify fine micron ranges (often 14–15.5 μm, sometimes finer) and request grade documentation per lot.
- **Lot consistency**: Programs tend to favour suppliers that can deliver consistent micron range, length and down content across multiple deliveries within a season.
- **Ply and construction**: The Japan market has a strong preference for 2-ply and 12-gauge knitwear, with seasonal variation between thicker gauge for autumn/winter and finer gauge for spring layering.
- **Yarn twist and hand-feel**: Japanese knitters and brand product teams are typically hand-feel-conscious. Yarn sample swatches are often requested before bulk order confirmation.
- **Documentation**: Beyond the standard invoice and packing list, Japanese buyers may request certificate of origin, fibre declaration and, for some programs, an explicit "Mongolian cashmere" origin statement.
- **Lead time and seasonality**: Programs are typically planned 6–9 months ahead, with autumn/winter deliveries peaking in July–September for arrival in October–November.

For an overview of how Ordos-origin cashmere fits into these programs, see the [from pasture to garment guide](/en/blog/from-pasture-to-garment-23-steps-ordos-cashmere/).

#### South Korea — growth segment, K-fashion-led, direct sourcing

The Korean cashmere knitwear import market has expanded as K-fashion brands have grown globally. The buyer landscape includes:

- **Mid- to high-end Korean brands** sourcing directly from Inner Mongolia for premium programs.
- **Cashmere specialists and ODM factories** in Korea working with both Korean and Japanese buyers.
- **Online-first brands** that market cashmere knitwear as a premium category, often with a transparent pricing and origin narrative.

Key practical considerations for Korea-bound cashmere programs:

- **Direct sourcing**: Korean brands are more likely to source directly from the mill or the dehairing facility, rather than through a trading house, in line with the trend toward transparent origin claims.
- **Lot traceability**: Several Korean brands ask for per-lot fibre origin records, including farm region and dehairing facility, in line with the broader traceability trend.
- **Yarn selection**: Korean buyers tend to specify 14–15.5 μm micron range for premium programs; some also work with 15.5–16.5 μm for entry-level lines.
- **Lead time**: Korean programs tend to be planned 4–6 months ahead, slightly shorter than Japan, with greater willingness to sample across multiple options.
- **Documentation**: Korean buyers typically request certificate of origin and fibre declaration; some also request specific labelling language for the consumer-facing tag.

For the underlying fibre-origin discussion relevant to both markets, see [how to identify premium cashmere](/en/blog/how-to-identify-premium-cashmere/).

#### Common practical records for both markets

The following records are typically worth confirming in writing for any Japan- or Korea-bound cashmere program, regardless of the specific buyer:

| Area | Practical record | Why it is useful now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Origin | Region (Ordos, Alashan, other Inner Mongolia sub-region) and herd type | Supports premium positioning and brand claims |
| Fibre grade | Micron range, length, down percentage | Supports hand-feel and quality claims |
| Lot reference | Lot or shipment reference linked to origin | Supports traceability per delivery |
| Composition | Per-style fibre declaration, including any blend components | Supports labelling and import declaration |
| Care guidance | Approved care label wording in the destination language | Supports product use and warranty claims |
| Documentation owner | Which party is responsible for each record | Clarifies the data request process |

These are administrative controls, not guarantees of any specific outcome. The actual scope, evidence and label wording depend on the buyer's brand policy and the destination's regulatory requirements.

#### How this fits with broader cashmere B2B trends

The Japan and Korea cashmere import markets are affected by the same frameworks as the EU market — traceability requirements, sustainability substantiation and labelling obligations — though the specific dates and scope differ. For an overview of the EU frameworks, see the [EU Digital Product Passport update](/en/blog/eu-textile-dpp-registry-2026-update/) and the [EU CSDDD for textile supply chains](/en/blog/eu-csddd-textile-supply-chain-2026/).

For Asia-specific questions about cashmere grading, hand-feel and knit construction, see the [micron chart guide](/en/blog/cashmere-fiber-fineness-micron-chart-b2b/) and the [ply vs single-ply comparison](/en/blog/cashmere-2-ply-vs-single-ply-yarn-garment/).

#### Working notes

The figures in this note are directional and intended for B2B reference. Actual import volumes, market share and brand activity should be confirmed with the latest trade statistics and current buyer intelligence before being used in commercial planning. For specific buyer introductions or program briefs, contact us through the project inquiry page.

### EU Textile Digital Product Passport Update: What Is Confirmed in August 2026

*Published 2026-08-27*

A dated update for cashmere and apparel buyers on the EU Digital Product Passport registry, the textile timetable, and the product records worth preparing before textile-specific rules are adopted.

## The August 2026 position: framework activity is real; textile requirements are not final

The European Commission’s Digital Product Passport (DPP) registry became operational on 20 July 2026. The Commission describes the DPP as a digital container for product, component and material information, with information requirements defined by the legal act that applies to each product group. [1](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/digital-product-passport_en)

For textile apparel, the important distinction is between the operational DPP framework and future textile-specific rules. The Commission’s current indicative timeline places adoption of sector-specific DPP requirements for textiles in **Q3–Q4 2027**. The data points, access rights and product obligations for textiles therefore remain dependent on the future delegated act; they should not be presented as final requirements today. [1](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/digital-product-passport_en)

## What the Commission has actually said

On 17 July 2026, the Commission launched its DPP information page as a central reference for economic operators, authorities, consumers and other value-chain participants. It says that, depending on the product group, a DPP may cover composition, circularity, environmental impact, usage and maintenance, safety, end-of-life guidance and regulatory compliance. [2](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/news/new-digital-product-passport-dpp-web-page-launched-2026-07-17_en)

The Commission also makes clear that the DPP will be introduced progressively. Textiles are identified as a priority product group, but the content of any passport must follow the product-specific legislation rather than a generic textile checklist. [1](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/digital-product-passport_en) This matters for cashmere programs: a QR code, a fiber statement or a generic origin narrative is not by itself a completed textile DPP.

## A practical product-record checklist for cashmere programs

The current period is useful for building disciplined product records, not for claiming future compliance. A buyer and supplier can agree which of the following records are available for a given style, lot or shipment:

| Record area | Practical reference to agree in writing | Why it is useful now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product identity | Style code, internal SKU, product category and revision | Keeps samples, production records and later data requests aligned. |
| Listed composition | Fiber declaration and the approved specification version | Provides a clear reference for labeling and product communication. |
| Material linkage | Lot, yarn or material references where they are actually maintained | Helps distinguish a product-level claim from a general supplier statement. |
| Care and use | Approved care-label wording and maintenance information | Supports product communication without assuming a future DPP data field. |
| Documentation owner | The party responsible for each document and its revision date | Makes it easier to answer brand or importer data requests consistently. |

These are procurement controls, not a claim that a product is DPP-ready. The appropriate scope, evidence and legal responsibility depend on the product, destination and the legislation in force when the product is placed on the market.

## Questions to raise in an upcoming sourcing review

For a cashmere yarn, knitwear or accessory program intended for the EU, a useful brief can ask: Which product identifiers are stable through sampling and bulk production? Which material and color records can be linked to the approved style? Which party will own and retain the records? Which details are documented today, and which would require a new process? Agreeing these points in writing creates a clearer working file while the textile delegated act is still pending.

For product-level starting points, see the [cashmere yarn product records](/en/products/yarn/), [raw-material records](/en/raw-material/) and [garment development information](/en/garment-oem/). For an EU program, confirm the applicable legal requirements with qualified legal or compliance advisers before making a market claim.

## References

1. European Commission, [Digital Product Passport](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/digital-product-passport_en), accessed 27 August 2026.
2. European Commission, [New Digital Product Passport (DPP) web page launched](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/news/new-digital-product-passport-dpp-web-page-launched-2026-07-17_en), 17 July 2026.

### EU Update: New Rules on Unsold Apparel and Accessories Took Effect for Large Companies in July 2026

*Published 2026-08-27*

A dated overview of the European Commission’s 2026 measures on unsold apparel, clothing accessories and footwear, with practical record-keeping questions for cashmere brand and sourcing teams.

## What changed in July 2026

On 9 February 2026, the European Commission announced delegated and implementing measures under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) concerning unsold consumer products. The Commission states that the ban on destroying unsold apparel, clothing accessories and footwear applies to large companies from **19 July 2026**; medium-sized companies are expected to follow in 2030. [1](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/news/new-eu-rules-stop-destruction-unsold-clothes-and-shoes-2026-02-09_en)

The same Commission update says that large companies are already subject to disclosure requirements relating to discarded unsold consumer products, while the standardised disclosure format applies from February 2027. The legal details, derogations and company scope should be checked against the applicable regulations rather than inferred from a product category alone. [1](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/news/new-eu-rules-stop-destruction-unsold-clothes-and-shoes-2026-02-09_en)

## Why this matters to a cashmere sourcing brief

This change is not a claim about any particular brand, importer or supplier. It is a reason for parties that place apparel or accessories on the EU market to ask more precise questions about item identity, inventory status and end-of-life decisions. A cashmere program may involve finished knitwear, scarves, hats, gloves or other accessories; the applicable legal duties depend on the responsible economic operator and the facts of that program.

The Commission says the measures clarify limited, justified circumstances in which destruction may be permitted, such as safety reasons or product damage, and that national authorities will oversee compliance. [1](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/news/new-eu-rules-stop-destruction-unsold-clothes-and-shoes-2026-02-09_en) A sourcing partner should therefore not use a generic “circular” statement in place of a documented decision process.

## Records worth discussing before production

| Project record | Question to agree | Avoid assuming |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Style identification | Can the approved style, color and size range be identified consistently? | That a style code alone proves legal compliance. |
| Quantity records | Which party maintains order, shipment, return and unsold-goods records? | That the upstream maker controls the importer’s inventory. |
| Defect and safety process | How are damaged, non-conforming or safety-related goods recorded and reviewed? | That every damaged item can be handled in the same way. |
| Alternative pathways | Which resale, repair, donation, reuse or recycling options are commercially and legally available? | That a pathway is available in every destination. |
| Responsibility map | Who is responsible for the applicable EU disclosure or prohibition requirements? | That responsibility follows the purchase order automatically. |

The value of these records is operational clarity. They can help a buyer separate product specification, inventory ownership, returns handling and environmental communication before a program launches. They do not replace legal advice, national guidance or a contract allocation of responsibility.

## A useful August 2026 review question

For a new EU-facing cashmere program, ask the brand or importer: *Which entity places the finished goods on the EU market, and what information will that entity need from its suppliers to support its unsold-goods process?* The answer can be translated into a project-specific documentation list rather than a broad claim about disposal, returns or circularity.

For specification-led discussions, begin with [cashmere garment development](/en/garment-oem/) or [cashmere yarn product records](/en/products/yarn/), then confirm the applicable EU and destination-market requirements in writing.

## References

1. European Commission, [New EU rules to stop destruction of unsold clothes and shoes](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/news/new-eu-rules-stop-destruction-unsold-clothes-and-shoes-2026-02-09_en), 9 February 2026.

### Cashmere Test Report Checklist: How B2B Buyers Verify Fiber Claims

*Published 2026-08-25*

A practical cashmere test-report checklist for brand buyers: what to request, how to read fiber data, and when to verify labels before production.

## Start with a claim that can be tested

“Cashmere” is not a quality grade, a hand-feel description, or a substitute for a fiber-content declaration. For a buyer developing a private-label knitwear range, it should be treated as a claim that needs to match a product specification, a batch record, and—where the commercial risk warrants it—an independent test result.

That distinction matters most when a sample becomes a production order. A beautifully soft swatch can help to approve color and handle, but it does not on its own establish composition, fiber-diameter distribution, or whether a later bulk lot matches the approved standard. Build the verification process into the purchase specification before sampling, rather than trying to reconstruct it after goods are packed.

For U.S.-bound wool products, the Federal Trade Commission explains that the name **cashmere** is reserved for the fine, dehaired undercoat fiber of the cashmere goat. Its guidance also describes a 19-micron limit for average cashmere fiber diameter, a limit on fibers above 30 microns, and a maximum coefficient of variation around the mean of 24%. These are labeling-definition requirements—not a universal luxury ranking system—so buyers should not turn a single micron number into a shortcut for every performance or price decision. [1](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/cachet-cashmere-complying-wool-products-labeling-act)

> **Buyer principle:** Match every marketing or label claim to a defined specification, a document owner, and a batch or style reference.

## The cashmere test-report checklist

Request documents in layers. The exact package varies by product, market, and contract, but the following checklist creates a practical starting point for raw fiber, yarn, and finished-garment sourcing.

| Checkpoint | What to request | What it helps establish | Practical buyer question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Commercial specification | Signed product specification with composition, yarn count, gauge, weight, color, tolerances, and care-label wording | The standard against which production is approved | “Which approved sample and revision does this bulk lot follow?” |
| Fiber identity and content | Independent lab report or agreed testing plan for composition and, where appropriate, cashmere identification | Whether the commercial claim is supported by testing | “Does the report identify both the method and the tested sample?” |
| Diameter data | Average fiber diameter plus variation data, if fiber fineness is part of the contract | Consistency with the agreed raw-material specification | “Is this a lot-specific result or a general capability statement?” |
| Lot traceability | Lot number, supplier/buying-station records, dehairing or spinning batch references, and material movement record | Whether the documents relate to the actual goods | “Can the mill link this cone, fabric roll, or garment lot to its source material?” |
| Finished-product controls | Measurement chart, shade approval, appearance/defect standard, and final-inspection record | Whether the finished item meets the approved production specification | “Who signs the release before shipment, and what is the rework path?” |
| Claim and label review | Artwork or label proof showing fiber percentages, origin statement, care instructions, and responsible business identity as required by the destination market | That consumer-facing claims match the approved composition | “Has the label been checked for the destination market before printing?” |

This is a sourcing checklist, not a substitute for market-specific legal advice or a laboratory method selection. For a U.S. program, the FTC notes that importers and sellers remain responsible for accurate labels and that periodic testing by a qualified independent laboratory is the best way to help assure fiber-content accuracy. [1](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/cachet-cashmere-complying-wool-products-labeling-act)

## Read the test method before comparing a number

An average micron result is only useful when the buyer knows what was sampled and how it was measured. ASTM D2130-22 describes a microprojection procedure for determining average fiber diameter and diameter variation for wool and other animal fibers, including cashmere, and states that the method is suitable for acceptance testing of commercial shipments when the parties use comparable sampling and testing. [2](https://store.astm.org/d2130-22.html)

The report should therefore be read as a chain rather than an isolated value:

1. **Sample identity.** Confirm the laboratory sample ID, lot number, material form, date received, and any sealing or chain-of-custody information. A result from a development lot cannot automatically be carried over to every future production batch.
2. **Method and scope.** Ask whether the report measures diameter, fiber identity, quantitative composition, or more than one property. One test does not necessarily answer every question.
3. **Result and variation.** Record the reported average together with the measure of variation used by the laboratory. Variation has commercial meaning because it affects how consistently a specification can be met.
4. **Decision rule.** State in the purchase order what happens when the result is outside tolerance: hold for review, re-test an agreed retained sample, downgrade, rework, or reject. Do not leave the consequence to a post-shipment negotiation.

The FTC further notes that trained experts can distinguish cashmere from sheep’s wool by optical or electron microscopy following AATCC or ASTM procedures, and that diameter alone is not the complete distinction because some sheep produce very fine fibers as well. [1](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/cachet-cashmere-complying-wool-products-labeling-act) This is why a supplier’s verbal “micron grade” is not a complete identity test.

## Separate fiber data from product performance

Fiber fineness, length, spinning construction, knit gauge, finishing, garment weight, dyeing, and use conditions all contribute to the garment a customer receives. A lower reported average fiber diameter may support a particular raw-material specification, but it does not automatically guarantee less pilling, better recovery, warmer wear, or a higher retail position.

For product development, translate a fiber requirement into an end-product brief. A good brief may specify the composition declaration, target yarn construction, gauge, garment weight, dimensional tolerances, pilling-test requirement where commercially relevant, approved hand-feel reference, and wash/care pathway. The corresponding factory release should then tie the finished style back to the approved sample and raw-material lot records.

Buyers comparing yarn should also ask for the commercial unit and processing stage. A test result on dehaired fiber, a yarn technical sheet, and a finished-sweater test report are related documents, but they are not interchangeable. See the site’s [cashmere grades guide](/en/cashmere-grades/) for a buyer-oriented starting point on fiber descriptors, then ask the supplier to define the actual tolerance and test plan in the specification.

## Treat sustainability and traceability claims as evidence requests

Responsible-sourcing language should be as specific as a composition claim. It is more useful to ask “which standard, which scope, which site, which certificate period, and which transaction records?” than to accept broad language such as “eco-friendly” or “fully traceable.”

Two industry reference points illustrate why scope matters. The Good Cashmere Standard describes an independent standard intended to address goat welfare, herders’ working conditions, and environmental protection, with independent audits at farms and production sites. [3](https://thegoodcashmerestandard.org/) The Sustainable Fibre Alliance’s Animal Fibre Standard identifies five principles: animal welfare, biodiversity and responsible land use, decent work, fiber-quality improvement, and an effective management system. [4](https://sustainablefibre.org/the-sfa-animal-fibre-standard/)

Neither reference means that every cashmere supplier or every lot is certified. A buyer should only make a certification-related product claim after checking the certificate holder, scope, validity, material flow, and any applicable transaction documentation. If certification is not part of the program, the supplier can still document traceability through lot records, processing records, and an agreed audit or disclosure process; the claim should describe exactly that evidence and no more.

## Build the review into three purchase gates

The most workable process is not to demand every document at the end. Instead, place the right review at three points in the buying cycle.

| Purchase gate | Buyer approval focus | Documents to retain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before sampling | Commercial intent and product definition | Technical pack, target composition, intended market, test-plan request, sample brief |
| Before bulk production | Material choice and claim readiness | Approved sample, bill of materials, lot references, lab-plan agreement, label proof |
| Before shipment | Conformity of finished goods and shipment documents | Final inspection record, packing list, final label artwork, lot traceability file, any agreed test reports |

This sequence reduces a common B2B failure mode: approving samples for appearance while leaving fiber verification, label copy, and responsibility for non-conforming results undecided until the delivery window is already closing.

## Questions to send with a quotation request

Use precise questions that a factory, yarn spinner, or trading partner can answer in writing:

- What is the proposed composition, and what evidence supports it for the production lot?
- Which material lot or yarn lot will be used for the sample, and how will bulk lots be identified?
- Which test methods are proposed for composition, fiber identity, or diameter if the contract requires them?
- Does the quoted price include the agreed test plan, retained samples, and a final inspection record?
- Which destination-market labels are the buyer responsible for approving, and when is artwork locked?
- If a result falls outside the written tolerance, what re-test, rework, credit, or rejection process applies?

For an RFQ that starts from raw fiber or top, visit [Cashmere Raw Material](/en/raw-material/). For yarn construction and material discussions, use the [Cashmere Yarn Product Records](/en/products/yarn/). For an apparel technical pack, label review, and production sequence, begin with [Cashmere Garment OEM/ODM](/en/garment-oem/).

## Final takeaway

The strongest cashmere claim is not the broadest one; it is the one a buyer can trace from product specification to batch record and, when needed, to an appropriate independent test. Ask for documents early, identify the exact sample each document represents, and agree the acceptance rule before bulk production begins. This produces a cleaner audit trail for the buyer, clearer instructions for the factory, and more credible product information for the eventual customer.

If you are preparing a cashmere RFQ, [contact our B2B team](/en/contact/) with the product category, target composition, destination market, expected quantity, and required test or documentation package. We can use that brief to structure the sampling and production documentation discussion before a quote is finalized.

## References

1. U.S. Federal Trade Commission, [Cachet of Cashmere: Complying with the Wool Products Labeling Act](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/cachet-cashmere-complying-wool-products-labeling-act).
2. ASTM International, [D2130-22: Standard Test Method for Diameter of Wool and Other Animal Fibers by Microprojection](https://store.astm.org/d2130-22.html).
3. Aid by Trade Foundation, [The Good Cashmere Standard](https://thegoodcashmerestandard.org/).
4. Sustainable Fibre Alliance, [The SFA Animal Fibre Standard](https://sustainablefibre.org/the-sfa-animal-fibre-standard/).

### B2B Cashmere Color Card Request: How to Get Samples & Timeline

*Published 2026-08-21*

Learn the exact information to send for a cashmere color card request, how to receive physical samples, and realistic B2B sample timelines from an Ordos source factory.

# B2B Cashmere Color Card Request: How to Get Samples & Timeline

## B2B Cashmere Color Card Request: What to Send, How to Get Samples, and Timeline Expectations

When you're sourcing cashmere for a wholesale collection, a color card is not just a piece of paper—it's the bridge between your design vision and production reality. For B2B buyers, requesting a color card from a cashmere supplier like us (DONGXIAO Cashmere, based in Ordos, Inner Mongolia) is a critical first step. But many importers make costly mistakes: they send vague emails, expect instant samples, or don't know what information accelerates the process.

This guide covers everything you need to know about B2B cashmere color card requests—what to include in your inquiry, how to receive physical samples, and realistic timelines at every stage. By the end, you'll know exactly how to streamline your sampling process and avoid delays.

### Why a Color Card Matters for Wholesale Cashmere

A cashmere color card is a swatch book or fan deck that displays the available dye colors for cashmere yarn, fabric, or finished garments. For a B2B buyer, it serves three purposes:

- **Color accuracy**: Digital screens are notoriously unreliable for matching shades. A physical card ensures your team and our production team see the same color.
- **Material quality**: You can feel the hand-feel, thickness, and fiber quality—something no PDF can replicate.
- **Production planning**: Color cards often indicate which shades are standard (low MOQ) versus custom (higher MOQ).

At DONGXIAO, our color cards are built on decades of experience dyeing cashmere in Ordos, where the finest Inner Mongolian fibers are processed. Every card includes 40–60 standard shades, plus options for custom Pantone matching.

### What to Send in Your B2B Color Card Request

To get the right color card and samples quickly, your initial request should be specific. Here’s a checklist of what to include:

1. **Your company profile** – Name, country, and business type (importer, brand, trading company). This helps us tailor the response.
2. **Product category** – Are you sourcing raw cashmere fiber, yarn, fabric, or finished garments? Each has a different color card format.
3. **Target fiber specifications** – If known, specify micron count (e.g., 15.5–16.5 microns), yarn count (e.g., 2/28 NM), or fabric weight (e.g., 220 GSM). This narrows down the card.
4. **Quantity estimates** – Your estimated annual or per-order volume. This informs MOQ discussions and whether we can send a full card or a smaller set.
5. **Color preferences** – If you have a Pantone reference or a brand palette, mention it. We can highlight matching shades on the card.
6. **Shipping address** – Physical address for courier delivery. Note that we ship worldwide via DHL, FedEx, or UPS.
7. **Timeline expectations** – When do you need the card? This helps us prioritize.

**Example inquiry**:

> Subject: Color Card Request for 2/28 NM Cashmere Yarn
> 
> Hi, we are a knitwear brand in Japan importing 5,000 kg of cashmere yarn annually. We need a color card for 2/28 NM, 15.5–16.5 micron yarn. Please send standard shades and advise if you can match Pantone 19-4020. Our address is [Tokyo, Japan]. We need this by next month.

### How to Receive Physical Samples: Step-by-Step

Once you send a complete request, here’s what happens at our factory:

- **Step 1: Review and confirm** – Our export team reviews your request within 1–2 business days. We may ask clarifying questions if anything is missing.
- **Step 2: Prepare the color card** – We compile the relevant card (yarn, fabric, or garment). Standard cards are always in stock.
- **Step 3: Ship via courier** – We ship using your preferred courier or our default (DHL). You receive a tracking number.
- **Step 4: Follow-up** – After you review, we schedule a call to discuss color matches, MOQs, and next steps.

**Important**: For standard color cards, we provide them free of charge to serious B2B buyers, but you may be asked to cover shipping costs (approximately $30–$60 depending on destination). For custom color matching (e.g., Pantone-specific shades), a small sample fee may apply, which is fully refundable against your first production order.

### Timeline Expectations for B2B Cashmere Samples

Timelines are the most common source of frustration in B2B sampling. Here’s a realistic breakdown based on our operations in Ordos, Inner Mongolia:

| Sample Type | Preparation Time | Shipping Time (Global) | Total Typical Timeline |
|-------------|------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Standard color card (stock) | 1–2 business days | 3–5 business days | 4–7 business days |
| Custom color card (dyed to match) | 5–7 business days | 3–5 business days | 8–12 business days |
| Yarn sample (from stock) | 2–3 business days | 3–5 business days | 5–8 business days |
| Fabric swatch (from stock) | 3–5 business days | 3–5 business days | 6–10 business days |
| Custom yarn/fabric development | 2–4 weeks | 3–5 business days | 2–5 weeks |
| Garment sample (pre-production) | 3–5 weeks | 3–5 business days | 4–6 weeks |

**Note**: These timelines assume standard specifications and no customs delays. During peak season (May–August for yarn orders), sample preparation may take 2–3 extra days.

### Factors That Affect Sample Speed

Several variables can speed up or delay your sample request:

- **Stock availability**: Standard colors are always in stock. Custom colors require dyeing, which takes longer.
- **Fiber specifications**: If you request a non-standard micron count (e.g., 14.5 microns), we may need to source special lots, adding 1–2 weeks.
- **Quantity of samples**: Requesting 20 swatches vs. 5 swatches affects preparation time.
- **Seasonality**: Our factory runs production year-round, but sample requests spike before trade shows (e.g., Pitti Filati, Première Vision). Plan ahead.
- **Customs and shipping**: International shipping is usually reliable, but some countries have stricter customs inspections. We recommend using express couriers to minimize delays.

### How to Get Color-Matched Samples (Custom Development)

If your brand requires exact Pantone or brand-specific colors, here’s the process:

1. **Send your color reference** – Provide Pantone codes, hex codes, or physical swatches.
2. **Lab dip** – We dye small yarn/fabric samples to match your reference. This takes 5–7 business days.
3. **Approval** – You review lab dips under daylight and artificial light. We may adjust the formula (1–2 rounds).
4. **Production sample** – Once approved, we create a full-size sample for your bulk order.

**Cost**: Lab dips are typically $50–$100 per color, but at DONGXIAO, we waive this fee for orders above 500 kg per color. All custom sample costs are deducted from your first production invoice.

### What to Do After Receiving Your Color Card

Once your card arrives, don’t just file it away. Use it strategically:

- **Evaluate hand-feel**: Compare the swatch against your quality standards. Cashmere should feel soft, not prickly.
- **Test color fastness**: Rub the swatch on a white cloth to check for dye transfer. High-quality dyeing (as per OEKO-TEX standards) should not bleed.
- **Check fiber content**: Ask for a certificate of analysis to confirm 100% cashmere (or your specified blend).
- **Plan your collection**: Use the card to shortlist colors that align with your market trends.

If you need additional swatches for your design team, just ask—we can send duplicate cards at cost.

### Why Source from DONGXIAO Cashmere in Ordos?

Ordos, Inner Mongolia, is the heart of the world’s finest cashmere production. Our factory has been operating here for 23 years, giving us direct access to premium raw cashmere and deep expertise in dyeing and spinning. We hold ISO9001 for quality management, OEKO-TEX Standard 100 for harmful substances, and GOTS certification for organic cashmere. When you request a color card from us, you’re not just getting colors—you’re getting a partnership with a source factory that controls the entire supply chain, from raw fiber to finished garment.

### Common Mistakes to Avoid in B2B Sample Requests

To ensure a smooth process, steer clear of these pitfalls:

- **Vague requests**: “Send me your color card” without context leads to generic responses. Specify your product category.
- **Ignoring MOQ**: Some buyers request custom colors without realizing the MOQ (usually 200–300 kg per color for yarn). Ask upfront.
- **Assuming instant turnaround**: Sampling takes time. Plan 2–4 weeks ahead of your production schedule.
- **Not checking shipping costs**: International shipping can be $50–$100. Confirm who bears the cost.
- **Overlooking certifications**: If you need GOTS or OEKO-TEX documentation, request it during sampling, not after production starts.

### Cashmere Micron Count Guide: 14.5-19.5μm for B2B Buyers

*Published 2026-08-20*

Understand cashmere fiber fineness with our practical micron guide. Learn grading, quality control, and sourcing tips for 14.5-19.5μm cashmere.

# Cashmere Micron Count Guide: 14.5-19.5μm for B2B Buyers

# Cashmere Fiber Fineness: A Practical Micron Guide for B2B Buyers (14.5-19.5μm)

When sourcing cashmere, the micron count is arguably the most critical specification—it determines softness, price, and end-use suitability. Yet many buyers struggle to interpret fineness data, especially when comparing suppliers across regions. This guide provides a comprehensive, practical breakdown of cashmere micron ranges, grading standards, and quality control considerations, empowering you to make informed sourcing decisions.

## What Is Cashmere Micron Count?

Micron (μm) measures fiber diameter. The lower the micron, the finer and softer the cashmere. Cashmere fibers range from about 14.5 to 19.5 microns, with anything below 15.5 considered ultra-fine and highly premium. For context, human hair is roughly 70-100 microns, so cashmere is exceptionally fine.

Fineness directly impacts:
- **Softness** – finer fibers feel silkier against the skin.
- **Durability** – finer fibers can be more delicate, requiring careful spinning.
- **Price** – finer cashmere commands higher prices due to lower yields and higher processing costs.
- **End-use** – ultra-fine cashmere is ideal for luxury knitwear, while coarser grades suit heavier outerwear.

## Cashmere Micron Grading: The Industry Standard

While there is no universal grading system, most mills and suppliers categorize cashmere into three tiers:

| Grade | Micron Range | Typical Use | Relative Price Index |
|-------|--------------|-------------|----------------------|
| Ultra-fine | ≤ 15.5 μm | Luxury scarves, lightweight knitwear, baby garments | High (100-120) |
| Fine | 15.6-16.5 μm | Premium sweaters, cardigans, accessories | Medium-High (90-100) |
| Standard | 16.6-18.5 μm | Everyday knitwear, blended yarns | Medium (75-90) |
| Coarse | 18.6-19.5 μm | Outerwear, blankets, upholstery | Lower (60-75) |

Note: Some suppliers may label 16-17 μm as "premium"—always verify the exact micron range in your specification sheet.

### Why 14.5-19.5 μm Matters for B2B Buyers

As a B2B buyer, you need to match micron to your product line and price point. For example:
- If you sell luxury women's knitwear retailing above $300, you'll want 15-16 μm cashmere.
- For men's sweaters in the mid-range, 16-17 μm is standard.
- For cost-effective blends, 18-19 μm works well, especially when combined with silk or wool.

Understanding the micron range helps you negotiate pricing, set quality expectations, and avoid overpaying for unnecessary fineness.

## How Micron Count Is Measured

The most reliable method is **laser-based optical fiber diameter analysis** (OFDA) or **scanning electron microscopy** (SEM). These methods provide accurate average micron and standard deviation. Some suppliers may use projection microscopy, which is less precise. Always request the testing method and a certificate of analysis (COA) from your supplier.

**Key metrics to request:**
- Average micron (μm)
- Standard deviation (SD) – lower SD means more uniform fibers
- Coefficient of variation (CV%) – typically below 22% is good
- Fiber length (mm) – longer fibers (34-40 mm) are better for spinning

## Regional Variations in Cashmere Fineness

Cashmere goats are raised in several regions, each with distinct fiber characteristics:

- **Inner Mongolia, China** – the world's largest cashmere producer. The Ordos region, where our factory is based, is renowned for consistently fine fibers averaging 15-16 μm. The harsh climate and high altitude (1,000-1,500m) contribute to a fine undercoat.
- **Mongolia** – similar quality to Inner Mongolia, with some variation depending on herding practices.
- **Afghanistan/Iran** – often coarser, averaging 17-19 μm, but with good availability.
- **Australia/New Zealand** – limited production, but fine fibers due to selective breeding.

As a source factory in Ordos, Inner Mongolia, we have direct access to the finest raw cashmere in the world, with an average micron of 15.5 μm for our premium line.

## Quality Control: What to Look For in a Supplier

Beyond micron count, quality control (QC) ensures consistency. A reliable supplier should:

1. **Provide COAs** for every batch, including micron, length, and contamination levels.
2. **Conduct third-party testing** – such as SGS or Intertek – upon request.
3. **Adhere to international standards** – ISO9001 for quality management, OEKO-TEX for chemical safety, and GOTS if you require organic certification.
4. **Maintain traceability** – from herder to finished product.

### Common Quality Defects to Watch For

- **Coarse hair contamination** – guard hairs that aren't fully removed.
- **High vegetable matter** – plant debris that affects spinning.
- **Inconsistent micron** – high SD indicates poor sorting.
- **Short fibers** – below 30 mm reduces yarn strength.

At DONGXIAO Cashmere, we implement rigorous QC at every stage: raw material sorting, dehairing, dyeing, and spinning. Our state-of-the-art testing lab ensures each batch meets your exact micron specification.

## Sourcing Strategies: How to Use Micron Data in Negotiations

When comparing supplier quotes, don't just look at price per kg. Evaluate the cost per garment based on micron and yield. Finer cashmere may cost more per kg but could require less material for the same warmth-to-weight ratio.

**Negotiation tips:**
- Request a sample card with swatches of different micron grades.
- Ask for a trial batch with your required micron and test it in your own lab.
- Inquire about blending options – adding 10-20% silk can enhance luster without increasing micron.
- Discuss MOQ flexibility – our factory offers MOQs starting from 200 kg for raw material, 500 kg for yarn, and 500 pieces per design for garments.

## Case Study: Selecting Micron for a Luxury Knitwear Line

A European brand approached us to develop a premium knitwear line. They wanted a soft, lightweight feel but had a target retail price of $250. We recommended a 15.8 μm cashmere with a 34 mm fiber length. This allowed a 12-gauge knit that was both fine and durable. We provided a COA showing a CV of 18%, ensuring evenness. The line launched successfully, with customer satisfaction rates above 95%.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Is lower micron always better?**
A: Not necessarily. Ultra-fine fibers (14.5-15 μm) can pill more easily and are more expensive. Match micron to your product's intended use and price point.

**Q: How does micron affect pilling?**
A: Finer fibers are more prone to pilling because they break and tangle. However, proper spinning and finishing (e.g., anti-pilling treatment) can mitigate this.

**Q: Can you provide custom micron blends?**
A: Yes, we can blend different micron lots to achieve a target average, but this may affect uniformity. We recommend using single-lot for premium products.

## Conclusion

Understanding cashmere micron count is essential for B2B buyers to source quality, control costs, and meet market expectations. By using this guide, you can confidently evaluate suppliers, interpret specifications, and negotiate better deals.

At DONGXIAO Cashmere, we offer a full range of cashmere products—from raw material and yarn to finished garments—with transparent micron specifications and rigorous quality control. Our factory in Ordos, Inner Mongolia, has 23 years of expertise, serving clients worldwide.

### Cashmere Baby Blanket vs Cashmere Baby Set: B2B Buyer's Guide to Manufacturing and Pricing

*Published 2026-08-18*

Cashmere baby blankets and cashmere baby sets are both high-margin gift items but have different manufacturing specs. B2B buyer's guide to choosing between blanket-only or full gift set, with MOQ, pricing, and target customer segments.

# Cashmere Baby Blanket vs Cashmere Baby Set: B2B Buyer's Guide

Cashmere baby products are a high-margin gift category, with retail prices of $150–600 for premium gift sets. Two product formats dominate: the cashmere baby blanket (single piece) and the cashmere baby set (blanket + matching hat, booties, or socks). Each format targets different customer segments and has different manufacturing specs.

This guide helps B2B buyers choose between blanket-only and full gift set, with MOQ, pricing, and target markets from a 23-year Ordos cashmere factory.

## Format 1: Cashmere Baby Blanket

A cashmere baby blanket is a single-piece product, typically 80×100 cm or 100×120 cm. Common formats:

**Receiving blanket (80×100 cm)**: Soft, lightweight, used for newborn wrapping. 100–150g per piece.

**Crib blanket (100×120 cm)**: Larger, slightly heavier, suitable for crib use. 200–280g per piece.

**Stroller blanket (75×90 cm)**: Compact size for stroller use. 150–200g per piece.

## Format 2: Cashmere Baby Set

A cashmere baby set combines the blanket with one or more matching pieces:

**2-piece set**: Blanket + matching hat
**3-piece set**: Blanket + matching hat + matching booties (most popular)
**4-piece set**: Blanket + hat + booties + socks
**5-piece set**: Blanket + hat + booties + socks + mittens

Each component uses the same yarn and color, creating a curated gift presentation.

## Which Format to Choose

- Customers want a single meaningful gift
- Retail price point under $300 is critical

**Choose cashmere baby set when**:
- Customers want a complete coordinated gift
- Retail price point $300–800 is acceptable

- The set is sold as a "new baby gift" or "first birthday gift"

## Target Customer Segments

**Wholesale baby boutiques**: Specialty baby stores with premium positioning. MOQ 50–200 pieces per SKU. Often work on smaller batch sizes with quick replenishment.

## Common Mistakes B2B Buyers Make

**Mistake 1: Using adult-grade yarn for baby products.** Cashmere baby products should use extra-fine yarn (2/48 Nm or finer) for softer hand-feel against sensitive skin. Adult yarn (2/26 Nm) feels coarse on babies.

**Mistake 2: Skipping OEKO-TEX certification.** Baby products worn against sensitive skin must be OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified. Without certification, retailers cannot sell to baby stores.

**Mistake 3: Using harsh dyes or chemicals.** Cashmere baby products should be dyed with low-impact, OEKO-TEX certified dyes. Standard reactive dyes can leave residues that irritate baby skin.

**Mistake 4: Inadequate gift box packaging.** Cashmere baby sets are bought as gifts. Without proper gift box, the perceived value drops 30–40%. Budget USD 3–6 per set for branded rigid gift boxes.

**Mistake 5: Skipping care instructions.** Cashmere baby products are bought by parents unfamiliar with cashmere care. Include a small care card with wash and storage instructions to prevent damage and complaints.

## Sustainability Considerations

Cashmere baby products require the highest sustainability standards:
- OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification (mandatory for baby products)
- Sustainable Fibre Alliance (SFA) certification
- Low-impact dyes (no azo dyes, no formaldehyde)
- Recycled cashmere blends (70% virgin / 30% recycled)
- Plastic-free packaging

These add USD 1–4 per piece but are essential for premium positioning.

### EU Digital Product Passport for Cashmere Garments: What B2B Exporters Must Prepare Before 2027

*Published 2026-08-18*

The EU's Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) entered force in July 2024, with the first Digital Product Passport (DPP) delegated acts for textiles expected in 2027. A working guide for cashmere B2B exporters: what data you must collect, who carries the cost, the realistic implementation timeline, and what we have already done at our Ordos facility.

# EU Digital Product Passport for Cashmere Garments: What B2B Exporters Must Prepare Before 2027

If you sell cashmere garments or accessories into the EU — directly to a brand, through a distributor, or via an online marketplace — the Digital Product Passport (DPP) will affect your compliance burden before the end of 2027. This is not a forecast; it is the published timeline of the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR), Regulation (EU) 2024/1781, which entered force on 18 July 2024.

The first DPP delegated act for textiles is scheduled for adoption by the European Commission in Q4 2026, with application beginning 18 months after publication — that puts the realistic go-live for textile DPPs in **mid-to-late 2027**. For B2B cashmere exporters who already work with EU brands on sustainability claims, this is the right time to start preparing the data systems, not when the regulation lands.

This guide covers what is known today (August 2026), what remains uncertain, and what we have already implemented at our Ordos facility for our existing EU customers. It is not legal advice — treat it as a working draft that you verify against current ESPR delegated acts as they publish.

## 1. What the Digital Product Passport Is

A DPP is a machine-readable digital record that travels with a physical product throughout its lifecycle. For textiles, the published DPP scope (per the ESPR working group outputs as of early 2026) is expected to include:

- **Product identification**: SKU, style number, batch/lot identifier, manufacturing date
- **Composition**: fiber content with percentages, country of origin per fiber stage
- **Manufacturing**: facility identification, country of manufacture, key process steps
- **Compliance**: REACH SV, compliance, OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification reference, other standards referenced on the care label
- **Durability and repair**: care instructions, expected lifespan guidance, repair service availability where applicable
- **End-of-life**: recycling instructions, take-back program reference (where required by national law)
- **Supply chain actors**: tier-1 supplier (the manufacturer), tier-2 (yarn supplier), tier-3 (fiber supplier), with country identifiers

The DPP is **not** a physical document attached to the garment. It is a digital record — typically a JSON or GS1-compatible Web URI — that EU customs, market surveillance authorities, and recyclers can access by scanning a data carrier (most likely a QR code on the care label or hangtag) on the physical product.

For B2B cashmere exporters, the practical impact is that each unique SKU you ship into the EU will need a DPP accessible via a unique identifier. For high-volume programs (1,000+ pieces per SKU), the data is the same per production batch. For small-batch or made-to-order programs (50–200 pieces per SKU), the data is unique per batch — which is operationally more demanding.

## 2. Implementation Timeline — What Is Known

The ESPR was published in the Official Journal on 28 June 2024 and entered force on 18 July 2024. The framework regulation does NOT specify textile DPP requirements directly. Instead, it authorizes the European Commission to adopt **delegated acts** that specify the DPP technical requirements per product group.

**Working timeline** (based on Commission work program as of August 2026):

- **Q4 2026**: First delegated act for textiles expected for adoption. This act will specify the data fields, the data carrier format, and the registry system for textile DPPs.
- **Mid-to-late 2027**: Application begins 18 months after delegated act publication. From this date, textile products placed on the EU market need a compliant DPP.
- **2028–2030**: Gradual extension to additional product groups (footwear, furniture, electronics already covered under ESPR working groups).

The "18 months after delegated act" timeline was confirmed in ESPR Article 77. This is the regulatory floor — it is unlikely to be delayed, but the Commission could in theory delay delegated act adoption by 6–12 months if industry pushback is significant. For B2B planning purposes, **2027 H2 is the realistic deadline**.

For cashmere specifically, two additional regulatory layers interact with DPP:

1. **EU Strategy for Sustainable and Circular Textiles** (March 2022) — the political framework that prompted ESPR
2. **Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)** — applies to large EU companies requiring supply chain due diligence on human rights and environmental impact. Cashmere herder welfare, land-use impact, and water consumption are within scope.

These two frameworks do not require a DPP directly, but they create the data demands that the DPP is designed to satisfy. B2B buyers that already comply with CSDDD will be the early adopters of DPP requirements from their suppliers.

## 3. What Data You Need to Collect for a Cashmere DPP

Based on the ESPR framework and the early delegated act drafts circulated to industry working groups in 2025–2026, the data fields expected for a cashmere garment DPP fall into five categories:

### Product identification
- Style number / SKU (your internal code is fine)
- Product type (sweater, scarf, blanket, etc.) — using the CN 2025 product classification or equivalent
- Fiber composition with percentages (e.g. "100% cashmere" or "70% cashmere / 30% merino wool")
- Net weight in grams (finished garment weight, excluding packaging)
- Color name and approximate Pantone code (for B2B traceability, not for visual reproduction)

### Origin and supply chain
- Country of fiber origin (where the cashmere goats were raised — for our facility, this is Inner Mongolia, China)
- Country of dehairing and combing (where raw fiber is processed into tops)
- Country of yarn spinning (where tops are spun into yarn)
- Country of knitting or weaving (where fabric or garment is constructed)
- Country of finishing (where dyeing, washing, or other finishing occurs)
- Country of final assembly (if different from knitting/weaving)

For vertically-integrated facilities like ours (dehairing, spinning, knitting, finishing all under one roof in Ordos), most fields point to "China — Inner Mongolia." For multi-tier supply chains, each tier requires its own evidence chain.

### Compliance and certification references
- OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certificate number (we hold certificate number available on request)
- REACH SV, compliance declaration (we maintain current SV, declarations for all EU shipments)
- Any other certification referenced on the care label (GOTS if organic, GRS if recycled, etc.)
- Testing lab accreditation references for any third-party verified content claims

### Care and durability
- Fiber care instructions (the standard care symbols plus a text version)
- Expected lifespan guidance (e.g. "with proper care, expected lifespan 8+ years for regular use")
- Repair service availability statement (e.g. "repair service available through [brand] or via our Ordos facility for wholesale customers")

### End-of-life
- Recycling instructions by material component
- Take-back program reference if you offer one (we do for wholesale customers shipping 5,000+ pieces annually)
- Disassembly guidance for complex garments (multi-material assembly)

For most cashmere garments, the data is straightforward to compile because cashmere is a single-fiber product. The complexity comes from blended products (cashmere + merino, cashmere + silk) where each fiber requires its own supply chain trace.

## 4. Who Carries the Compliance Burden

ESPR Article 7 places the **primary obligation** on the "manufacturer" — defined as the person who places the product on the EU market, whether manufactured in the EU or imported.

For B2B cashmere exports, this means:

- **If you sell to an EU brand who then sells under their own label**: the EU brand is the "manufacturer" under ESPR and carries primary compliance. You, as the upstream supplier, are expected to provide the data they need to construct the DPP.
- **If you ship cashmere to an EU distributor or importer who sells under your brand name**: your brand name on the product makes you the "manufacturer" under ESPR. The EU importer becomes your "authorized representative" for compliance but you retain primary data ownership.
- **If you sell to an EU consumer via cross-border e-commerce (DTC)**: you are the manufacturer and carry full DPP obligation.

In practice, the cost of constructing a DPP per SKU is small (typically €0.05–€0.50 per SKU depending on data complexity and whether you use the official EU registry or a GS1-compatible private registry). The cost is in **data collection and verification**, not in the registry infrastructure itself.

For B2B exporters, the realistic approach is to provide a DPP data dossier to your EU customer per shipment, and let them handle the actual DPP registration. This is consistent with how OEKO-TEX and REACH compliance documentation already works.

## 5. What We Have Already Implemented at Our Ordos Facility

We started DPP preparation in Q1 2025 when the ESPR working group drafts first circulated. As of August 2026, the following is operational for our EU customers:

**Tier-1 (our facility)**: every garment SKU produced since January 2025 carries a unique batch identifier traceable to the production date, machine, and operator shift. We can pull a per-SKU data dossier within 48 hours of request.

**Tier-2 (our yarn production)**: every yarn batch carries a fiber origin declaration (country of goat raising), dehairing date, and spinning date. We maintain these records for 7 years per EU customs requirements.

**Tier-3 (fiber sourcing)**: we work with 12 contracted herder cooperatives in Alashan and Ordos, each with a fiber origin certificate. The 2026 SFA (Sustainable Fibre Alliance) certification cycle added chain-of-custody documentation that satisfies most of the upstream traceability expectations in the ESPR framework.

**OEKO-TEX and REACH**: we maintain current OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification for our facility and products, and current REACH SV, declarations for all EU shipments.

**Data carrier**: we are piloting GS1 Digital Link QR codes on care labels for one EU customer program starting Q3 2026. The QR code resolves to a JSON document hosted on our wholesale portal that contains the per-SKU data dossier.

We expect to be ready for the textile DPP delegated act application date (mid-to-late 2027) without significant additional investment. The cost has been mainly in our internal data systems and the SFA certification fees — not in any new physical infrastructure.

## 6. Practical Steps for Cashmere B2B Exporters

If you are shipping cashmere to the EU today and you have not started DPP preparation, the work falls into three tiers over the next 12–18 months:

**By Q4 2026** (immediate):
- Audit your current data systems against the ESPR framework requirements. Identify which fields you can produce today and which require new data collection.
- Talk to your EU customers about their DPP expectations. Most large EU brands are running internal DPP pilots in 2026 — they will tell you what data they need from you.
- If you are not currently OEKO-TEX certified, start the certification process. OEKO-TEX Standard 100 is the most universally accepted baseline for textile DPPs.

**By Q2 2027** (within 10 months):
- Establish data carrier format for your SKUs (likely GS1 Digital Link QR code on care label or hangtag).
- Build a per-SKU data dossier generation process. This can be a simple spreadsheet-driven process for small catalogs or a dedicated PLM integration for catalogs of 500+ SKUs.
- If you operate in a multi-tier supply chain (fiber sourced separately from spinning, etc.), start collecting tier-2 and tier-3 data now. Tier-3 fiber origin documentation is the slowest part to assemble.

**By Q4 2027** (before delegated act application):
- Complete DPP registration per SKU with your chosen registry (EU registry when available, or GS1-compatible private registry in the meantime).
- Update your commercial terms to reference DPP readiness as a sales argument for EU buyers.
- Brief your QC and shipping teams on DPP data capture in the production workflow.

For B2B buyers: if your EU customer is asking about DPP, they are likely a brand preparing for the 2027 deadline. Treat this as a long-term partnership signal — they are investing in the relationship.

## 7. What Remains Uncertain

Several aspects of the textile DPP are not yet finalized as of August 2026:

- **Exact data fields** for the first textile delegated act (expected Q4 2026 publication)
- **Registry system** — whether the EU will mandate the official EU registry or accept GS1-compatible private registries
- **Data carrier format** — QR code vs NFC vs both
- **Repair service definition** — what counts as "available" for small-batch producers
- **Cost structure** for multi-tier supply chains with no traceability infrastructure

The Commission is publishing draft delegated acts for stakeholder consultation during 2026, with final adoption expected late 2026 or early 2027. The implementation details may shift before the regulation lands, so plan for a flexible data schema rather than committing to one technical format too early.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### When does the textile DPP actually start applying?

The first textile DPP delegated act is expected for adoption by the European Commission in Q4 2026. Application begins 18 months after publication — that puts the realistic go-live for textile DPPs in mid-to-late 2027. For B2B planning purposes, treat Q4 2027 as the operational deadline.

### Who pays for the DPP infrastructure?

The ESPR places the compliance obligation on the manufacturer (the entity placing the product on the EU market). For B2B cashmere exports to EU brands, the brand typically carries primary DPP obligation. Your cost is in providing the data dossier per shipment, which is small per SKU (€0.05–€0.50 depending on complexity).

### Do I need to redo my compliance documentation for DPP?

No. DPP integrates with existing compliance frameworks (OEKO-TEX Standard 100, REACH SV, declarations, ISO 9001, SFA certification). You reference your existing certifications in the DPP rather than obtaining new ones. The work is in data integration, not in obtaining new compliance documentation.

### Can I use my own data carrier format for DPP?

The ESPR delegated act is expected to specify the data carrier format. The most likely format is GS1 Digital Link QR code (already widely deployed in EU retail). Plan for QR code on care label or hangtag. Pilot with one EU customer before scaling.

### What happens if I do not have a DPP for products shipped to the EU after the delegated act applies?

Market surveillance authorities can require withdrawal or recall of non-compliant products. For B2B exports, this typically surfaces as your EU customer refusing shipment. The compliance cost of late preparation is significantly higher than the cost of early preparation.

### Does DPP apply to products manufactured before the delegated act applies?

No. DPP applies to products placed on the EU market after the application date. Existing inventory and products manufactured before the application date are not under DPP requirement unless they are placed on the market after the date.

### How does DPP interact with CSDDD (Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive)?

CSDDD requires large EU companies to conduct supply chain due diligence on human rights and environmental impact. DPP provides the data infrastructure that CSDDD compliance can rely on. For cashmere, herder welfare, land use, and water consumption are within CSDDD scope. If you already work with EU brands on CSDDD compliance, DPP data collection should integrate with your existing CSDDD workflow.

### Private Label Cashmere Gloves: B2B Manufacturing Guide (Lining, Embroidery, MOQ)

*Published 2026-08-18*

Private label cashmere gloves require fine-gauge knit construction (12-16 gauge) and proper lining integration. B2B buyer's guide to manufacturing private label cashmere gloves: gauge, lining, embroidery, MOQ, and target markets.

# Private Label Cashmere Gloves: B2B Manufacturing Guide

Cashmere gloves are a high-margin private label category, with retail prices of $80–250 per pair and gift set bundles reaching $300–500. They occupy a unique position in cashmere apparel — small enough for individual gifting, luxurious enough for premium positioning, and versatile enough to work across men's and women's lines.

This guide covers manufacturing specifications, lining options, embroidery, MOQ, and target customer segments from a 23-year Ordos cashmere factory.

## Why Cashmere Gloves Are a Strong Private Label Category

Three reasons B2B buyers should consider cashmere gloves:

**High perceived value**: Gloves are a small-ticket item compared to sweaters and coats, but cashmere gloves feel like a significant gift. Retail markup of 4–6x is standard.

**Year-round demand**: Cashmere gloves work for fall, winter, and early spring. They also work indoors for cold offices and travel.

**Cross-gender appeal**: A well-designed cashmere glove in neutral colors appeals to men, women, and unisex buyers. Easy to expand into men's lines without redesigning.

## Standard Cashmere Glove Specifications

| Specification | Standard | Premium |
|---|---|---|
| Fiber | Grade A Mongolian 14.5–15.5μm | Grade A+ 14.5μm |
| Yarn count | 2/48 Nm worsted-spun | 2/60 Nm worsted-spun |
| Gauge | 12 gauge | 14 or 16 gauge (finer) |
| Construction | Plain knit | Plain knit with ribbed cuff |
| Weight per pair | 30–45g | 45–60g |
| Sizes | One-size fits most | S/M/L/XL plus custom |
| Lining | Unlined | Cashmere, merino, or silk lined |
| Color | Stock 12 Pantone shades | Custom Pantone |
| Retail price | $80–150 | $150–250 |

## Gauge and Hand-Feel

**12 gauge**: Standard cashmere glove construction. Soft, drapey, warm. Suitable for everyday cold-weather wear.

**14 gauge**: Finer gauge produces a more refined, dressier glove. Slightly lighter. More expensive per piece but feels more premium.

**16 gauge**: Ultra-fine gauge for the most refined cashmere glove. Very lightweight (35–45g per pair). Suitable for indoor and mild-winter wear. Most expensive per piece.

Higher gauge = more knitting time = higher cost. 14 gauge adds 15–25% to per-piece price; 16 gauge adds 30–50%.

## Lining Options

**Unlined**: Standard cashmere glove. Soft against skin but limited insulation for very cold climates.

**Cashmere-lined**: Double-layer construction with cashmere interior. Warmest option. Adds USD 3–6 per pair but premium retail pricing.

**Merino-lined**: Wool interior with cashmere exterior. Warm and durable. Adds USD 2–4 per pair. Most popular for cold-climate markets.

**Silk-lined**: Silk interior with cashmere exterior. Refined, dressy, suitable for formal wear. Adds USD 2–5 per pair.

**Cashmere-silk blend lined**: Mid-price option that combines the warmth of cashmere with the smoothness of silk. Adds USD 3–5 per pair.

## Embroidery and Customization

**Embroidered logo on cuff**: Most common customization. From 100 pairs. Embroidery preserves the cashmere hand-feel better than printed labels.

**Embroidered initials on back of hand**: Premium customization for monogram programs. From 200 pairs. Adds USD 1–3 per pair.

**Custom Pantone**: From 5 kg per color. Lab dip in 5–7 days, bulk production 25–30 days after approval.

**Custom buttons or clasps**: For gauntlet-style or convertible mittens. From 200 pairs. Adds USD 2–5 per pair.

**Custom gift box**: Branded rigid box with tissue, ribbon, and care card. From 500 pairs. Adds USD 3–6 per set.

## MOQ and Lead Time

**MOQ**: 100 pairs per design in stock colors. Custom Pantone from 5 kg per color. Lined versions from 200 pairs. Custom sizing from 300 pairs per size run.

**Lead time**: 25–35 days bulk production + 3–5 days QC + 20–35 days sea freight.

**Sample timeline**: 7–10 days for sample sets at USD 30–80 per pair, refundable against first bulk order.

## Target Customer Segments

**Premium gift retailers**: Cashmere gloves as standalone luxury gifts, often bundled in sets with cashmere scarves or hats. MOQ 100–500 pairs per SKU.

**Department stores**: Department store private label programs. MOQ 500–2,000 pairs per SKU. Custom packaging and labeling.

**Men's specialty stores**: Refined cashmere gloves in classic colors (black, navy, charcoal, brown). MOQ 100–500 pairs per SKU. Often sold with matching cashmere scarf.

**Outdoor and travel brands**: Cashmere-lined or merino-lined cashmere gloves for cold-weather travel. MOQ 200–500 pairs per SKU. Focus on warmth and durability.

**Corporate gifting**: Branded cashmere gloves for executive gifts. MOQ 100–500 pairs per event. Custom packaging with brand logo.

## Common Mistakes B2B Buyers Make

**Mistake 1: Selling cashmere gloves as workwear.** Cashmere gloves are not designed for heavy outdoor use. Marketing them as "ski gloves" or "work gloves" creates unrealistic expectations. Position as luxury everyday gloves.

**Mistake 2: Not specifying gauge in the inquiry.** Cashmere factories can produce 12, 14, or 16 gauge construction. Gauge significantly affects hand-feel and price. Always specify.

**Mistake 3: Skipping the ribbed cuff.** A ribbed cuff holds the glove in place without elastic. Plain knit cuffs slip and require constant adjustment. Worth the USD 0.50–1.00 per pair upgrade.

**Mistake 4: Not testing lining for cold climates.** A cashmere glove without proper lining is suitable for mild winters only. For Nordic/Russian/Canadian markets, specify cashmere-lined or merino-lined construction.

**Mistake 5: Underestimating packaging costs.** Premium cashmere gloves sold as gifts require premium packaging. Rigid gift boxes add USD 3–6 per set — significant for a $80 retail product.

## Sustainability Considerations

Cashmere glove buyers increasingly expect:
- OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification
- Sustainable Fibre Alliance (SFA) certification
- Recycled cashmere blends (70% virgin / 30% recycled)
- FSC-certified packaging
- Reusable storage pouch (replaces single-use plastic packaging)

These add USD 0.50–2.00 per pair but enable premium positioning.

### What is the best gauge for cashmere gloves?

12 gauge for everyday cold-weather wear (most common). 14 gauge for dressier, refined gloves (premium positioning). 16 gauge for ultra-fine indoor or mild-winter gloves (most expensive).

Yes. Embroidered logo on the cuff from 100 pairs (most common). Embroidered initials on the back of the hand from 200 pairs. Custom woven labels from 100 pairs. Custom gift box from 500 pairs.
